entries.a62507d9bbe2dfa4106a554d5d3d90ae1c350174: <div sID="gen16445" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="44" osisID="Isa.44" sID="Isa.44"/> <div eID="gen16445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16446" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16447" type="x-p"/> God, by the prophet, goes on in this chapter, as before, I. To encourage his people with the assurance of great blessings he had in store for them at their return out of captivity, and those typical of much greater which the gospel church, his spiritual Israel, should partake of in the days of the Messiah; and hereby he proves himself to be God alone against all pretenders, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1-Isa.44.8">ver. 1-8</reference>. II. To expose the sottishness and amazing folly of idol-makers and idol-worshippers, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9-Isa.44.20">ver. 9-20</reference>. III. To ratify and confirm the assurances he had given to his people of those great blessings, and to raise their joyful and believing expectations of them, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.21-Isa.44.28">ver. 21-28</reference>.
entries.03134bcef170edd5d1d654fdebc60a4a566bc0e0: <div eID="gen16447" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16446" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prosperity Foretold; The Supremacy of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16448" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Yet now hear, O Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen: <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that made thee, and formed thee from the womb, <hi type="italic">which</hi> will help thee; Fear not, O Jacob, my servant; and thou, Jesurun, whom I have chosen. <hi type="super">3</hi> For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring: <hi type="super">4</hi> And they shall spring up <hi type="italic">as</hi> among the grass, as willows by the water courses. <hi type="super">5</hi> One shall say, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's; and another shall call <hi type="italic">himself</hi> by the name of Jacob; and another shall subscribe <hi type="italic">with</hi> his hand unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and surname <hi type="italic">himself</hi> by the name of Israel. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the King of Israel, and his redeemer the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the first, and I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the last; and beside me <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no God. <hi type="super">7</hi> And who, as I, shall call, and shall declare it, and set it in order for me, since I appointed the ancient people? and the things that are coming, and shall come, let them show unto them. <hi type="super">8</hi> Fear ye not, neither be afraid: have not I told thee from that time, and have declared <hi type="italic">it?</hi> ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> even my witnesses. Is there a God beside me? yea, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no God; I know not <hi type="italic">any.</hi> <div eID="gen16448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16449" type="x-p"/> Two great truths are abundantly made out in these verses:— <div eID="gen16449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16450" type="x-p"/> I. That the people of God are a happy people, especially upon account of the covenant that is between them and God. The people of Israel were so as a figure of the gospel Israel. Three things complete their happiness:— <div eID="gen16450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16451" type="x-p"/> 1. The covenant-relations wherein they stand to God, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1-Isa.44.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Israel is here called <hi type="italic">Jeshurun—the upright one;</hi> for those only, like Nathanael, are Israelites indeed, in whom is no guile, and those only shall have the everlasting benefit of these promises. Jacob and Israel had been represented, in the close of the foregoing chapter, as very provoking and obnoxious to God's wrath, and already given to the curse and to reproaches; but, as if God's bowels yearned towards him and his repentings were kindled together, mercy steps in with a <hi type="italic">non-obstante—notwithstanding,</hi> to all these quarrels: "<hi type="italic">Yet now, hear, O Jacob my servant!</hi> thou and I will be friends again for all this." God had said (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">ch. xliii. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am he that blotteth out thy transgression,</hi> which is the only thing that creates this distance; and when that is taken away the streams of mercy run again in their former channel. The pardon of sin is the inlet of all the other blessings of the covenant. So and so I will do for them, says God (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.12">Heb. viii. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">for I will be merciful to their unrighteousness.</hi> Therefore <hi type="italic">hear, O Jacob!</hi> hear these comfortable words; therefore <hi type="italic">fear not, O Jacob!</hi> fear not thy troubles, for by the pardon of sin the property of them too is altered. Now the relations wherein they stand to him are very encouraging. (1.) They are his <hi type="italic">servants;</hi> and those that serve him he will own and stand by and see that they be not wronged. (2.) They are his <hi type="italic">chosen,</hi> and he will abide by his choice; he knows those that are his, and those whom he has chosen he takes under special protection. (3.) They are his creatures. He <hi type="italic">made them,</hi> and brought them into being; he <hi type="italic">formed them,</hi> and cast them into shape; he began betimes with them, for he <hi type="italic">formed them from the womb;</hi> and therefore he will help them over their difficulties and help them in their services. <div eID="gen16451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16452" type="x-p"/> 2. The covenant-blessings which he has secured to them and theirs, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3-Isa.44.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. (1.) Those that are sensible of their spiritual wants, and the insufficiency of the creature to supply them, shall have abundant satisfaction in God: <hi type="italic">I will pour water upon him that is thirsty,</hi> that thirsts after righteousness; he shall be filled. Water shall be poured out to those who truly desire spiritual blessings above all the delights of sense. (2.) Those that are barren as the dry ground shall be watered with the grace of God, with floods of that grace, and God will himself give the increase. If the ground be ever so dry, God has floods of grace to water it with. (3.) The water God will pour out is <hi type="italic">his Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.7.39">John vii. 39</reference>), which God will pour out without measure upon the seed, that is, Christ (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.16">Gal. iii. 16</reference>), and by measure upon all the seed of the faithful, upon all the praying wrestling seed of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.13">Luke xi. 13</reference>. This is the great New-Testament promise, that God, having sent his servant Christ, and upheld him, will send his Spirit to uphold us. (4.) This gift of the Holy Ghost is the great blessing God had reserved the plentiful effusion of for the latter days: <hi type="italic">I will pour my Spirit,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">my blessing;</hi> for where God gives his Spirit he will give all other blessings. (5.) This is reserved for the seed and offspring of the church; for so the covenant of grace runs: <hi type="italic">I will be a God to thee and to thy seed.</hi> To all who are thus made to partake of the privileges of adoption God will give the spirit of adoption. (6.) Hereby there shall be a great increase of the church. Thus it shall be spread to distant places. Thus it shall be propagated and perpetuated to after-times: <hi type="italic">They shall spring up</hi> and grow as fast <hi type="italic">as willows by the watercourses,</hi> and in every thing that is virtuous and praiseworthy shall be eminent and excel all about them, as the willows overtop the grass among which they grow, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.4">v. 4</reference>. Note, It is a great happiness to the church, and a great pleasure to good men, to see the rising generation hopeful and promising. And it will be so if God pour his Spirit upon them, that blessing, that blessing of blessings. <div eID="gen16452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16453" type="x-p"/> 3. The consent they cheerfully give to their part of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">v. 5</reference>. When the Jews returned out of captivity they renewed their covenant with God (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jer. l. 5</reference>), particularly that they would have no more to do with idols, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.2-Hos.14.3">Hos. xiv. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">8</reference>. Backsliders must thus repent and do their first works. Many of those that were without did at that time join themselves to them, invited by that glorious appearance of God for them, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Esth. viii. 17</reference>. And they say, <hi type="italic">We are the Lord's</hi> and <hi type="italic">call themselves by the name of Jacob;</hi> for there was one law, one covenant, <hi type="italic">for the stranger and for those that were born in the land.</hi> And doubtless it looks further yet, to the conversion of the Gentiles, and the multitudes of them who, upon the effusion of the Spirit, after Christ's ascension, should be <hi type="italic">joined to the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">added to the church.</hi> These converts are <hi type="italic">one and another,</hi> very many, of different ranks and nations, and all welcome to God, <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col. iii. 11</reference>. When one does it another shall by his example be invited to do it, and then another; thus the zeal of one may provoke many. (1.) They shall resign themselves to God: not one in the name of the rest, but every one for himself shall say, "<hi type="italic">I am the Lord's;</hi> he has an incontestable right to rule me, and I submit to him, to all his commands, to all his disposal. I am, and will be, his only, his wholly, his for ever, will be for his interests, will be for his praise; living and dying I will be his." (2.) They shall incorporate themselves with the people of God, <hi type="italic">call themselves by the name of Jacob,</hi> forgetting their own people and their fathers' house, and desirous to wear the character and livery of God's family. They shall love all God's people, shall associate with them, give them the right hand of fellowship, espouse their cause, seek the good of the church in general and of all the particular members of it, and be willing to take their lot with them in all conditions. (3.) They shall do this very solemnly. Some of them shall <hi type="italic">subscribe with their hand unto the Lord,</hi> as, for the confirming of a bargain, a man sets his hand to it, and delivers it as his act and deed. The more express we are in our covenanting with God the better, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Exod. xxiv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.24.26-Josh.24.27">Jos. xxiv. 26, 27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.38">Neh. ix. 38</reference>. Fast bind, fast find. <div eID="gen16453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16454" type="x-p"/> II. That, as the Israel of God are a happy people, so the God of Israel is a great God, and he is God alone. This also, as the former, speaks abundant satisfaction to all that trust in him, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6-Isa.44.8">v. 6-8</reference>. Observe here, to God's glory and our comfort, 1. That the God we trust in is a God of incontestable sovereignty and irresistible power. He is <hi type="italic">the Lord,</hi> Jehovah, self-existent and self-sufficient; and he is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all the hosts of heaven and earth, of angels and men. 2. That he stands in relation to, and has a particular concern for, his church. He is <hi type="italic">the King of Israel and his Redeemer; therefore</hi> his Redeemer because his King; and those that take God for their King shall have him for their Redeemer. When God would assert himself God alone he proclaims himself Israel's God, that his people may be encouraged both to adhere to him and to triumph in him. 3. That he is eternal—<hi type="italic">the first and the last.</hi> He is God from everlasting, before the worlds were, and will be so to everlasting, when the world shall be no more. If there were not a God to create, nothing would ever have been; and, if there were not a God to uphold, all would soon come to nothing again. He is all in all, is the first cause, from whom are all things, and the last end, to and for whom are all things (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.36">Rom. xi. 36</reference>), the <hi type="italic">Alpha and the Omega,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.1.11">Rev. i. 11</reference>. 4. That he is God alone (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Besides me there is no God. Is there a God besides me?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">v. 8</reference>. We will appeal to the greatest scholars. Did they ever in all their reading meet with any other? To those that have had the largest acquaintance with the world. Did they ever meet with any other? There are <hi type="italic">gods many</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.5-1Cor.8.6">1 Cor. viii. 5, 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">called gods,</hi> and counterfeit gods: but is there any besides our God that is infinite and eternal, any besides him that is the creator of the world and the protector and benefactor of the whole creation, any besides him that can do that for their worshippers which he can and will do for his? "<hi type="italic">You are my witnesses.</hi> I have been a nonsuch to you. You have tried other gods; have you found any of them all-sufficient to you, or any of them like me? <hi type="italic">Yea, there is no god," no rock</hi> (so the word is), none besides Jehovah that can be a rock for a foundation to build on, a rock for shelter to flee to. God is the rock, and <hi type="italic">their rock is not as ours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">Deut. xxxii. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.31">31</reference>. <hi type="italic">I know not any;</hi> as if he had said, "I never met with any that offered to stand in competition with me, or that durst bring their pretensions to a fair trial; if I did know of any that could befriend you better than I can, I would recommend you to them; but I know not any." There is no God besides Jehovah. He is infinite, and therefore there can be no other; he is all-sufficient, and therefore there needs no other. This is designed for the confirming of the hopes of God's people in the promise of their deliverance out of Babylon, and, in order to that, for the curing of them of their idolatry; when the affliction had done its work it should be removed. They are reminded of the first and great article of their creed, that <hi type="italic">the Lord their God is one Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.6.4">Deut. vi. 4</reference>. And therefore, (1.) They needed not to hope in any other god. Those on whom the sun shines need neither moon nor stars, nor the light of their own fire. (2.) They needed not to fear any other god. Their own God was more able to do them good than all the false and counterfeit gods of their enemies were to do them hurt. 5. That none besides could foretel these things to come, which God now by his prophet gave notice of to the world, above 200 years before they came to pass (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Who, as I, shall call,</hi> shall call Cyrus to Babylon? Is there any but God that can call effectually, and has every creature, every heart, at his beck? Who <hi type="italic">shall declare it,</hi> how it shall be, and by whom, as I do?" Nay, God goes further; he not only sees it in order, as having the foreknowledge of it, but <hi type="italic">sets it in order,</hi> as having the sole management and direction of it. Can any other pretend to this? He has always set things in order according to the counsel of his own will, ever <hi type="italic">since he appointed the ancient people,</hi> the people of Israel, who could give a truer and fuller account of the antiquities of their own nation than any other kingdom in the world could give of theirs. Ever since he appointed that people to be his peculiar people his providence was particularly conversant about them, and he told them beforehand the events that should occur respecting them—their bondage in Egypt, their deliverance from it, and their settlement in Canaan. All was set in order in the divine predictions as well as in the divine purposes. Could any other have done so? Would any other have been so far concerned for them? He challenges the pretenders to show the things that shall come hereafter: "Let them, if they can, tell us the name of the man that shall destroy Babylon ad deliver Israel? Nay, if they cannot pretend to tell us <hi type="italic">the things that shall come</hi> hereafter, let them tell us the things that <hi type="italic">are coming,</hi> that are nigh at hand and at the door. Let them tell us what shall come to pass to-morrow; but they cannot do that; fear them not therefore, nor be afraid of them. What harm can they do you? What hindrance can they give to your deliverance, when I have told thee it shall be accomplished in its season, and I have solemnly declared it?" Note, Those who have the word of God's promise to depend upon need not be afraid of any adverse powers or policies whatsoever.
entries.29d4eeed2f55e9ebdf0d824ab00cec01541186cb: <div eID="gen16454" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Folly of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16455" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> They that make a graven image <hi type="italic">are</hi> all of them vanity; and their delectable things shall not profit; and they <hi type="italic">are</hi> their own witnesses; they see not, nor know; that they may be ashamed. <hi type="super">10</hi> Who hath formed a god, or molten a graven image <hi type="italic">that</hi> is profitable for nothing? <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, all his fellows shall be ashamed: and the workmen, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> of men: let them all be gathered together, let them stand up; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> they shall fear, <hi type="italic">and</hi> they shall be ashamed together. <hi type="super">12</hi> The smith with the tongs both worketh in the coals, and fashioneth it with hammers, and worketh it with the strength of his arms: yea, he is hungry, and his strength faileth: he drinketh no water, and is faint. <hi type="super">13</hi> The carpenter stretcheth out <hi type="italic">his</hi> rule; he marketh it out with a line; he fitteth it with planes, and he marketh it out with the compass, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man; that it may remain in the house. <hi type="super">14</hi> He heweth him down cedars, and taketh the cypress and the oak, which he strengtheneth for himself among the trees of the forest: he planteth an ash, and the rain doth nourish <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">15</hi> Then shall it be for a man to burn: for he will take thereof, and warm himself; yea, he kindleth <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and baketh bread; yea, he maketh a god, and worshippeth <hi type="italic">it;</hi> he maketh it a graven image, and falleth down thereto. <hi type="super">16</hi> He burneth part thereof in the fire; with part thereof he eateth flesh; he roasteth roast, and is satisfied: yea, he warmeth <hi type="italic">himself,</hi> and saith, Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire: <hi type="super">17</hi> And the residue thereof he maketh a god, <hi type="italic">even</hi> his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my god. <hi type="super">18</hi> They have not known nor understood: for he hath shut their eyes, that they cannot see; <hi type="italic">and</hi> their hearts, that they cannot understand. <hi type="super">19</hi> And none considereth in his heart, neither <hi type="italic">is there</hi> knowledge nor understanding to say, I have burned part of it in the fire; yea, also I have baked bread upon the coals thereof; I have roasted flesh, and eaten <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and shall I make the residue thereof an abomination? shall I fall down to the stock of a tree? <hi type="super">20</hi> He feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, <hi type="italic">Is there</hi> not a lie in my right hand? <div eID="gen16455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16456" type="x-p"/> Often before, God, by the prophet, had mentioned the folly and strange sottishness of idolaters; but here he enlarges upon that head, and very fully and particularly exposes them to contempt and ridicule. This discourse is intended, 1. To arm the people of Israel against the strong temptation they would be in to worship idols when they were captives in Babylon, in compliance with the custom of the country (they being far from the city of their own solemnities) and to humour those who were now their lords and masters. 2. To cure them of their inclination to idolatry, which was the sin that did most easily beset them and to reform them from which they were sent into Babylon. As the rod of God is of use to enforce the word, so the word of God is of use to explain the rod, that the voice of both together may be heard and answered. 3. To furnish them with something to say to their Chaldean task-masters. When they insulted over them, when they asked, <hi type="italic">Where is your God?</hi> they might hence ask them, <hi type="italic">What are your gods?</hi> 4. To take off their fear of the gods of their enemies, and to encourage their hope in their own God that he would certainly appear against those who set up such scandalous competitors as these with him for the throne. <div eID="gen16456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16457" type="x-p"/> Now here, for the conviction of idolaters, we have, <div eID="gen16457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16458" type="x-p"/> I. A challenge given to them to clear themselves, if they can, from the imputation of the most shameful folly and senselessness imaginable, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9-Isa.44.11">v. 9-11</reference>. They set their wits on work to contrive, and their hands on work to frame, graven images, and they call them <hi type="italic">their delectable things;</hi> extremely fond they are of them, and mighty things they expect from them. Note, Through the corruption of men's nature, those things that should be detestable to them are desirable and delectable; but those are far gone in a distemper to whom that which is the food and fuel of it is most agreeable. Now, 1. We tell them that those that do so are all vanity; they deceive themselves and one another, and put a great cheat upon those for whom they make these images. 2. We tell them that <hi type="italic">their delectable things shall not profit</hi> them, nor make them any return for the pleasure they take in them; they can neither supply them with good nor protect them from evil. The <hi type="italic">graven images</hi> are <hi type="italic">profitable for nothing</hi> at all, nor will they ever get any thing by the devoirs they pay to them. 3. We appeal to themselves whether it be not a silly sottish thing to expect any good from gods of their own making: <hi type="italic">They are their own witnesses,</hi> witnesses against themselves, if they would but give their own consciences leave to deal faithfully with them, that they are blind and ignorant in doing thus. <hi type="italic">They see not nor know,</hi> and let them own it, <hi type="italic">that they may be ashamed.</hi> If men would but be true to their own convictions, ordinarily we might be sure of their conversion, particularly idolaters; for <hi type="italic">who has formed a god?</hi> Who but a mad-man, or one out of his wits, would think of forming a god, of making that which, if he make it a god, he must suppose to be his maker? 4. We challenge them to plead their own cause with any confidence or assurance. If any one has the front to say that he has formed a god, when all his fellows come together to declare what each of them has done towards the making of this god, they will all be ashamed of the cheat they have put upon themselves, and laugh in their sleeves at those whom they have imposed upon; for <hi type="italic">the workmen</hi> that formed this god <hi type="italic">are of men,</hi> weak and impotent, and therefore cannot possibly make a being that shall be omnipotent, nor can they without blushing pretend to do so. <hi type="italic">Let them all be gathered together,</hi> as Demetrius and the craftsmen were, to support their sinking trade; <hi type="italic">let them stand up</hi> to plead their own cause, and make the best they can of it, with hand joined in hand; <hi type="italic">yet they shall fear</hi> to undertake it when it comes to the setting to, as conscious to themselves of the weakness and badness of their cause, <hi type="italic">and they shall be ashamed</hi> of it, not only when they appear singly, but when by appearing together they hope to keep one another in countenance. Note, Idolatry and impiety are things which men may justly both tremble and blush to appear in the defence of. <div eID="gen16458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16459" type="x-p"/> II. A particular narrative of the whole proceeding in making a god; and there needs no more to expose it than to describe it and tell the story of it. <div eID="gen16459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16460" type="x-p"/> 1. The persons employed about it are handicraft tradesmen, the meanest of them, the very same that you would employ in making the common utensils of your husbandry, a cart or a plough. You must have a <hi type="italic">smith,</hi> a blacksmith, who <hi type="italic">with the tongs works in the coals;</hi> and it is hard work, for he <hi type="italic">works with the strength of his arms,</hi> till <hi type="italic">he is hungry</hi> and his strength fails, so eager is he, and so hasty are those who set him at the work to get it despatched. He cannot allow himself time to eat or drink, for <hi type="italic">he drinks no water, and</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">is faint,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12">v. 12</reference>. Perhaps it was a piece of superstition among them for the workman not to eat or drink while he was making a god. The plates with which the smith was to cover the image, or whatever iron-work was to be done about it, <hi type="italic">he fashioned with hammers,</hi> and made it all very exact, according to the model given him. Then comes <hi type="italic">the carpenter,</hi> and he takes as much care and pains about the timber-work, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.13">v. 13</reference>. He brings his box of tools, for he has occasion for them all: <hi type="italic">He stretches out his rule</hi> upon the piece of wood, <hi type="italic">marks it with a line,</hi> where it must be sawed or cut of; <hi type="italic">he fits it,</hi> or polishes it, <hi type="italic">with planes,</hi> the greater first and then the less; <hi type="italic">he marks out with the compasses</hi> what must be the size and shape of it; and it is just what he pleases. <div eID="gen16460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16461" type="x-p"/> 2. The form in which it is made is that of a man, a poor, weak, dying creature; but it is the noblest form and figure that he is acquainted with, and, being his own, he has a peculiar fondness for it and is willing to put all the reputation he can upon it. He makes it <hi type="italic">according to the beauty of a man,</hi> in comely proportion, with those limbs and lineaments that are the beauty of a man, but are altogether unfit to represent the beauty of the Lord. God put a great honour upon man when, in respect of the powers and faculties of his souls, he made him after the image of God; but man does a great dishonour to God when he makes him, in respect of bodily parts and members, after the image of man. Nor will it at all atone for the affront so far to compliment his god as to take the fairest of the children of men for his original whence to take his copy, and to give him all the beauty of a man that he can think of; for all the <hi type="italic">beauty of the body of a man,</hi> when pretended to be put upon him who is an infinite Spirit, is a deformity and diminution to him. And, when the goodly piece is finished, it must <hi type="italic">remain in the house,</hi> in the temple or shrine prepared for it, or perhaps in the dwelling house if it be one of the <hi type="italic">lares</hi> or <hi type="italic">penates—the household gods.</hi> <div eID="gen16461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16462" type="x-p"/> 3. The matter of which it is mostly made is sorry stuff to make a god of; it is the stock of a tree. <div eID="gen16462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16463" type="x-p"/> (1.) The tree itself was fetched out <hi type="italic">of the forest,</hi> where it grew among other trees, of no more virtue or value than its neighbours. It was a <hi type="italic">cedar,</hi> it may be, or a <hi type="italic">cypress,</hi> or an <hi type="italic">oak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.14">v. 14</reference>. Perhaps he had an eye upon it some time before for this use, and <hi type="italic">strengthened it for himself,</hi> used some art or other to make it stronger and better-grown than other trees were. Or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">which hath strengthened or lifted up itself among the trees of the forest,</hi> the tallest and strongest he can pick out. Or, it may be, it pleases his fancy better to take <hi type="italic">an ash,</hi> which is of a quicker growth, and which was of his own planting for this use, and which has been nourished with rain from heaven. See what a fallacy he puts upon himself, in making that his refuge which was of his own planting, and which he not only gave the form to, but prepared the matter for; and what an affront he puts upon the God of heaven in setting up that a rival with him which was nourished by his rain, that rain which falls upon the just and unjust. <div eID="gen16463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16464" type="x-p"/> (2.) The boughs of this tree were good for nothing but for fuel; to that use were they put, and so were the chips that were cut off from it in the working of it; they are <hi type="italic">for a man to burn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.15-Isa.44.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. To show that that tree has no innate virtue in it for its own protection, it is as capable of being burnt as any other tree; and, to show that he who chose it had no more antecedent value for it than for any other tree, he makes no difficulty of throwing part of it into the fire as common rubbish, asking no question for conscience' sake. [1.] It serves him for his parlour-fire: <hi type="italic">He will take thereof and warm himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">v. 15</reference>), and he finds the comfort of it, and is so far from having any regret in his mind for it that he saith, <hi type="italic">Aha! I am warm; I have seen the fire;</hi> and certainly that part of the tree which served him for fuel, the use for which God and nature designed it, does him a much greater kindness and yields him more satisfaction than ever that will which he makes a god of. [2.] It serves him for his kitchen-fire: <hi type="italic">He eats flesh</hi> with it, that is, he dresses the flesh with it which he is to eat; he <hi type="italic">roasteth roast, and is satisfied</hi> that he has not done amiss to put it to this use. Nay, [3.] It serves him to heat the oven with, in which we use that fuel which is of least value: <hi type="italic">He kindles it and bakes bread</hi> with the heat of it, and none charges him with doing wrong. <div eID="gen16464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16465" type="x-p"/> (3.) Yet, after all, the stock or body of the tree shall serve to make a god of, when it might as well have served to make a bench, as one of themselves, even a poet of their own, upbraids them, <hi type="italic">Horat. made use of for that purpose: <div eID="gen16476" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16477"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16478"/>Furaces moneo manus repellas,<l eID="gen16478" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16481"/>Drive the plunderers away, and preserve the wood for thy master's hearth, or thou thyself shalt be converted into fuel<hi type="small-caps">.—Martial.</hi><l eID="gen16481" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16477"/> <div sID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> When the besotted idolater has thus served the meanest purposes with part of his tree, and the rest has had time to season (he makes that a god in his imagination while that is in the doing, <hi type="italic">and worships it</hi>): He <hi type="italic">makes it a graven image, and falls down thereto</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">v. 15</reference>), that is (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">The residue thereof he makes a god, even his graven image,</hi> according to his fancy and intention; he <hi type="italic">falls down to it, and worships it,</hi> gives divine honours to it, prostrates himself before it in the most humble reverent posture, as a servant, as a suppliant; <hi type="italic">he prays to it,</hi> as having a dependence upon it, and great expectations from it; <hi type="italic">he saith, Deliver me, for thou art my god.</hi> There where he pays his homage and allegiance he justly looks for protection and deliverance. What a strange infatuation is this, to expect help from gods that cannot help themselves! But it is this praying to them that makes them gods, not what the smith or the carpenter did to them. What we place our confidence in for deliverance that we make a god of. <div eID="gen16482" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16483"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16484"/>Qui fingit sacros, auro vel marmore, vultus<l eID="gen16484" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16485"/>Non facit ille deos; qui rogat, ille facit.<l eID="gen16485" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16486"/>He who supplicates the figure, whether it be of gold or of<l eID="gen16486" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16487"/>marble, makes it a god, and not he who merely<l eID="gen16487" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16488"/>constructs it<hi type="small-caps">.—Martial.</hi><l eID="gen16488" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16483"/> <div sID="gen16489" type="x-p"/> III. Here is judgment given upon this whole matter, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.18-Isa.44.20">v. 18-20</reference>. In short, it is the effect and evidence of the greatest stupidity and sottishness that one could ever imagine rational beings to be guilty of, and shows that man has become worse than the beasts that perish; for they act according to the dictates of sense, but man acts not according to the dictates of reason (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">They have not known nor understood</hi> common sense; men that act rationally in other things in this act most absurdly. Though they have some knowledge and understanding, yet they are strangers to, nay, they are rebels against the great law of consideration (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">None considers in his heart,</hi> nor has so much application of mind as to reason thus with himself, which one would think he might easily do, though there were none to reason with him: "<hi type="italic">I have burnt part of this tree in the fire,</hi> for baking and roasting; <hi type="italic">and</hi> now <hi type="italic">shall I make the residue thereof an abomination?</hi>" (that is, <hi type="italic">an idol,</hi> for that is an abomination to God and all wise and good men); "shall I ungratefully choose to do, or presumptuously dare to do, what the Lord hates? shall I be such a fool as to fall down to the stock of a tree—a senseless, lifeless, helpless thing? shall I so far disparage myself, and make myself like that I bow down to?" A growing tree may be a beautiful stately thing, but the stock of a tree has lost its glory, and he has lost his that gives glory to it. Upon the whole, the sad character given of these idolaters is, 1. That they put a cheat upon themselves (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">They feed on ashes;</hi> they feed themselves with hopes of advantage by worshipping these idols, but they will be disappointed as much as a man that would expect nourishment by feeding on ashes. Feeding on ashes is an evidence of a depraved appetite and a distempered body; and it is a sign that the soul is overpowered by very bad habits when men, in their worship, go no further than the sight of their eyes will carry them. They are wretchedly deluded, and it is their own fault: <hi type="italic">A deceived heart</hi> of their own, more than the deceiving tongue of others, <hi type="italic">has turned them aside</hi> from the faith and worship of the living God to dumb idols. They are <hi type="italic">drawn away of their own lusts and enticed.</hi> The apostasy of sinners from God is owing entirely to themselves and to the evil heart of unbelief that is in their own bosom. A revolting and rebellious heart is a deceived heart. 2. That they wilfully persist in their self-delusion and will not be undeceived. There is none of them that can be persuaded so far to suspect himself as to say, <hi type="italic">Is there not a lie in my right hand?</hi> and so to think of delivering his soul. Note, (1.) Idolaters have a lie in their right hand; for an idol is a lie, is not what it pretends, performs not what it promises, and it is a <hi type="italic">teacher of lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">Hab. ii. 18</reference>. (2.) It highly concerns those that are secure in an evil way seriously to consider whether there be not a lie in their right hand. Is not that a lie which with complacency we hold fast as our chief good? Are our hearts set upon the wealth of the world and the pleasures of sense? They will certainly prove a lie in our right hand. And is not that a lie which with confidence we hold fast by, as the ground on which we build our hopes for heaven? If we trust to our external professions and performances, as if those would save us, we deceive ourselves with a lie in our right hand, with a house built on the sand. (3.) Self-suspicion is the first step towards self-deliverance. We cannot be faithful to ourselves unless we are jealous of ourselves. He that would deliver his soul must begin with putting this question to his own conscience. <hi type="italic">Is there not a lie in my right hand?</hi> (4.) Those that are given up to believe in a lie are under the power of strong delusions, which it is hard to get clear of, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.11">2 Thess. ii. 11</reference>.
entries.80d217987f0d9a3ad526c3481c28d76da796a82f: <div eID="gen16489" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to the People of God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 708.)</title> <div sID="gen16490" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> Remember these, O Jacob and Israel; for thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my servant: I have formed thee; thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my servant: O Israel, thou shalt not be forgotten of me. <hi type="super">22</hi> I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins: return unto me; for I have redeemed thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> Sing, O ye heavens; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath done <hi type="italic">it:</hi> shout, ye lower parts of the earth: break forth into singing, ye mountains, O forest, and every tree therein: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath redeemed Jacob, and glorified himself in Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thy redeemer, and he that formed thee from the womb, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that maketh all <hi type="italic">things;</hi> that stretcheth forth the heavens alone; that spreadeth abroad the earth by myself; <hi type="super">25</hi> That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish; <hi type="super">26</hi> That confirmeth the word of his servant, and performeth the counsel of his messengers; that saith to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be inhabited; and to the cities of Judah, Ye shall be built, and I will raise up the decayed places thereof: <hi type="super">27</hi> That saith to the deep, Be dry, and I will dry up thy rivers: <hi type="super">28</hi> That saith of Cyrus, <hi type="italic">He is</hi> my shepherd, and shall perform all my pleasure: even saying to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built; and to the temple, Thy foundation shall be laid. <div eID="gen16490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16491" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen16491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> I. The duty which Jacob and Israel, now in captivity, were called to, that they might be qualified and prepared for the deliverance designed them. Our first care must be to get good by our afflictions, and then we may hope to get out of them. The duty is expressed in two words: <hi type="italic">Remember</hi> and <hi type="italic">return,</hi> as in the counsel to Ephesus, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.4-Rev.2.5">Rev. ii. 4, 5</reference>. 1. "<hi type="italic">Remember these, O Jacob!</hi> Remember what thou hast been told of the folly of idolatry, and let the convictions thou art now under be ready to thee whenever thou art tempted to that sin. Remember that <hi type="italic">thou art my servant,</hi> and therefore must not serve other masters." 2. <hi type="italic">Return unto me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">v. 22</reference>. It is the great concern of those who have backslidden from God to hasten their return to him; and this is that which he calls them to when they are in affliction, and when he is returning to them in a way of mercy. <div eID="gen16492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> II. The favours which Jacob and Israel, now in captivity, were assured of; and what is here promised to them upon their remembering and returning to God is in a spiritual sense promised to all that in like manner return to God. It is a very comfortable word, for more is implied in it than is expressed (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O Israel! thou shalt not be forgotten of me,</hi> though for the present thou seemest to be so." When we begin to remember God he will begin to remember us; nay, it is he that remembers us first. Now observe here, <div eID="gen16493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> 1. The grounds upon which God's favourable intentions to his people were built and on which they might build their expectations from him. He will deliver them out of captivity; for, (1.) They are his servants, and therefore he has a just quarrel with those that detain them. <hi type="italic">Let my people go, that they may serve me.</hi> The servants of the King of kings are under special protection. (2.) He formed them into a people, formed them <hi type="italic">from the womb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">v. 24</reference>. From the first beginning of their increase into a nation they were under his particular care and government, more than any other people; their national constitution was of his framing, and his covenant with them was the charter by which they were incorporated. They are his, and he will save them. (3.) He has redeemed them formerly, has many a time redeemed them out of great distress, and he is still the same, in the same relation to them, has the same concern for them. "Therefore <hi type="italic">return unto me, for I have redeemed thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">v. 22</reference>. Whither wilt thou go, but to me?" Having redeemed them, as well as formed them, he has acquired a further title to them and propriety in them, which is a good reason why they should dutifully return to him and why he will graciously return to them. The <hi type="italic">Lord has redeemed Jacob;</hi> he is about to do it (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">v. 23</reference>); he has determined to do it; for he is the Lord their Redeemer, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">v. 24</reference>. Note, The work of redemption which God has by his Son wrought for us encourages us to hope for all promised blessings from him. He that has redeemed us at so vast an expense will not lose his purchase. (4.) He has <hi type="italic">glorified himself in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">v. 23</reference>), and therefore will do so still, <reference osisRef="John.12.28">John xii. 28</reference>. It is matter of comfort to us to see God's glory interested in the deliverances of the church; for <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he will certainly redeem Jacob, because thus he will glorify himself. And <hi type="italic">this</hi> assures us that he will perfect the redemption of his saints by Jesus Christ, because there is a day set when he will be glorified and admired in them all. (5.) He has pardoned their sins, which were the cause of their calamity and the only obstruction to their deliverance, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">v. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he will break the yoke of captivity from off their necks, because he has <hi type="italic">blotted out, as a thick cloud, their transgressions.</hi> Note, [1.] Our transgressions and our sins are as a cloud, a thick cloud; they interpose between heaven and earth, and for a time suspend and intercept the correspondence between the upper and lower world (sin <hi type="italic">separates between us and God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.2">ch. lix. 2</reference>); they threaten a storm, a deluge of wrath, as thick clouds do, which God will rain upon sinners. <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>. [2.] When God pardons sin he blots out this cloud, this thick cloud, so that the intercourse with heaven is laid open again. God looks down upon the soul with favour; the soul looks up to him with pleasure. The cloud is scattered by the influence of the Sun of righteousness. It is only through Christ that sin is pardoned. When sin is pardoned, like a cloud that is scattered, it appears no more, it is quite gone. The <hi type="italic">iniquity of Jacob shall be sought for, and not found,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.50.20">Jer. l. 20</reference>. And the comforts that flow into the soul when sin is pardoned are like the <hi type="italic">clear shining after clouds and rain.</hi> <div eID="gen16494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> 2. The universal joy which the deliverance of God's people should bring along with it (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Sing, O you heavens!</hi> This intimates, (1.) That the whole creation shall have cause for joy and rejoicing in the redemption of God's people; to that it is owing that it subsists (that it is rescued from the curse which the sin of man brought upon the ground) and that it is again put into a capacity of answering the ends of its being, and is assured that though now it groans, being burdened, it shall at last be delivered from the bondage of corruption. The greatest establishment of the world is the kingdom of God in it, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11-Ps.96.13">Ps. xcvi. 11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.7-Ps.98.9">xcviii. 7-9</reference>. (2.) That the angels shall rejoice in it, and the inhabitants of the upper world. The heavens shall sing, for the Lord has done it. And there is joy in heaven when God and man are reconciled (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.7">Luke xv. 7</reference>), joy when Babylon falls, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.20">Rev. xviii. 20</reference>. (3.) That those who lay at the greatest distance, even the inhabitants of the Gentile world, should join in these praises, as sharing in these joys. The <hi type="italic">lower parts of the earth,</hi> the forest and the trees there, shall bring in the tribute of thanksgiving for the redemption of Israel. <div eID="gen16495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> 3. The encouragement we have to hope that though great difficulties, and such as have been thought insuperable, lie in the way of the church's deliverance, yet, when the time for it shall come, they shall all be got over with ease; for <hi type="italic">thus saith Israel's Redeemer, I am the Lord that maketh all things,</hi> did make them at first and am still making them; for providence is a continued creation. All being, power, life, emotion, and perfection, are from God. He <hi type="italic">stretches forth the heavens alone,</hi> has no help nor needs any; and the earth too he <hi type="italic">spreads abroad by himself,</hi> and by his own power. Man was not by him when he did it (<reference osisRef="Job.38.4">Job xxxviii. 4</reference>), nor did any creature advise or assist; only his own eternal wisdom and Word was by him then as <hi type="italic">one brought up with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>. His stretching out the heavens by himself denotes the boundless extent of his power. The strongest man, if he has to stretch a thing out, must get somebody or other to lend a hand; but God stretched out the vast expanse and keeps it still upon the stretch, himself, by his own power. Let not Israel be discouraged then; nothing is too hard for him to do that made the world, <reference osisRef="Ps.124.8">Ps. cxxiv. 8</reference>. And, having made all things, he can make what use he pleases of all, and has it in his power to serve his own purposes by them. <div eID="gen16496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> 4. The confusion which this would put upon the oracles of Babylon, by the confutation it would give them, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.25">v. 25</reference>. God, by delivering his people out of Babylon, would <hi type="italic">frustrate the tokens of the liars,</hi> of all the lying prophets, that said the Babylonian monarchy had many ages yet to live, and pretended to ground their predictions upon some token, some sign or other, which, according to the rules of their arts, foreboded its prosperity. How mad will these conjurors grow with vexation when they see that their skill fails them, and that the contrary happens to that which they so coveted and were so confident of. Nor would it only baffle their pretended prophets, but their celebrated politicians too: He <hi type="italic">turns the wise men backward.</hi> Finding they cannot go on with their projects, they are forced to quit them; and so he makes the judges fools, <hi type="italic">and makes their knowledge foolish.</hi> Those that are made acquainted with Christ see all the knowledge they had before to be foolishness in comparison with the knowledge of him. And those that are adversaries to him will find all their counsels, like Ahitophel's, turned into foolishness, and themselves <hi type="italic">taken in their own craftiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.19">1 Cor. iii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen16497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> 5. The confirmation which this would give to the oracles of God, which the Jews had distrusted and their enemies despised: God <hi type="italic">confirms the word of his servant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">v. 26</reference>); he confirms it by accomplishing it in its season; and <hi type="italic">performs the counsel of the messengers</hi> whom he hath many a time sent to his people, to tell them what great blessings he had in store for them. Note, The exact fulfilling of the prophecies of scripture is a confirmation of the truth of the whole book and an incontestable evidence of its divine origin and authority. <div eID="gen16498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16499" type="x-p"/> 6. The particular favours God designed for his people, that were now in captivity, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26-Isa.44.28">v. 26-28</reference>. These were foretold long before they went into captivity, that they might see reason to expect a correction, but no reason to fear a final destruction. (1.) It is here supposed that Jerusalem, and the cities of Judah, should for a time lie in ruins, dispeopled and uninhabited; but it is promised that they shall be rebuilt and repeopled. When Isaiah lived, Jerusalem and the cities of Judah were full of inhabitants; but they will be emptied, burnt, and destroyed. It was then hard to believe that concerning such strong and populous cities. But the justice of God will do that; and, when that is done, it will be hard to believe that ever they will recover themselves again, and yet the zeal of the Lord of hosts will do that to. God has said to Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be inhabited;</hi> for, while the world stands, God will have a church in it, and therefore he will raise up those who <hi type="italic">shall say to Jerusalem, Thou shalt be built;</hi> for, if it be not built, it cannot be inhabited, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.35-Ps.69.36">Ps. lxix. 35, 36</reference>. When God's time shall have come for the building up of his church, let him alone to find both houses for his people (for they shall not lie exposed) and people for his houses, for they shall not stand empty. The cities of Judah too shall again be built. The Assyrian army under Sennacherib only took them, and then, upon the defeat of that army, they returned undamaged to the right owners; but the Chaldean army demolished them, and by carrying away the inhabitants left them to go to decay of themselves; for, if less judgments prevail not to humble and reform men, God will send greater. Yet these desolations shall not be perpetual. God will <hi type="italic">raise up the</hi> wastes and <hi type="italic">decayed places thereof;</hi> for he will not contend for ever. The city of strangers, when it is ruined, shall never be built (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">ch. xxv. 2</reference>), but the city of God's own children is but discontinued for a time. (2.) It is here supposed that the temple too should be destroyed, and lie for a time rased to the foundations; but it is promised that the foundation of it shall again be laid, and no doubt built upon. As the desolation of the sanctuary was to all the pious Jews the most mournful part of the destruction, so the restoration and re-establishment of it would be the most joyful part of the deliverance. What joy can they have in the rebuilding of Jerusalem if the temple there be not rebuilt? for it is that which makes it a holy city and truly beautiful. This therefore was the chief thing that the Jews had at heart and had in view in their return; therefore they would go back to Jerusalem, to <hi type="italic">build the house of the Lord God of Israel there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.3">Ezra i. 3</reference>. (3.) It is here supposed that very great difficulties would lie in the way of this deliverance, which it would be impossible for them to wade through; but it is promised that by a divine power they shall all be removed (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">God saith to the deep, Be dry;</hi> so he did when he brought Israel out of Egypt, and so he will again when he brings them out of Babylon, if there be occasion. <hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great mountain?</hi> Dost thou stand in the way? Before Zerubbabel, the commander-in-chief of the returning captives, <hi type="italic">thou shalt become a plain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.7">Zech. iv. 7</reference>. So, <hi type="italic">Who art thou, O great deep?</hi> Dost thou retard their passage and think to block it up? Thou shalt be dry, and thy rivers that supply thee shall be dried up. When Cyrus took Babylon by draining the river Euphrates into many channels, and so making it passable for his army, this was fulfilled. Note, Whatever obstructions lie in the way of Israel's redemption, God can remove them with a word's speaking. (4.) It is here supposed that none of the Jews themselves would be able by might and power to force their way out of Babylon but it is promised that God will raise up a stranger from afar off, that shall fairly open the way for them, and now at length he names the very man, many scores of years before he was born or thought of (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd.</hi> Israel is his people, and the sheep of his pasture. These sheep are now in the midst of wolves, in the hands of the thief and robber; they are impounded for trespass. Now Cyrus shall be his shepherd, employed by him to release these sheep, and to take care of their return to their own green pasture again. "In this <hi type="italic">he shall perform all my pleasure,</hi> shall bring about what is purposed by me and will be highly pleasing to me." Note, [1.] The most contingent things are certain to the divine prescience. He knew who was the person, and what was his name, that should be the deliverer of his people, and, when he pleased, he could let his church know it, that, when they heard of such a name beginning to be talked of in the world, they might <hi type="italic">lift up their heads with joy, knowing that their redemption drew nigh.</hi> [2.] It is the greatest honour of the greatest men to be employed for God as instruments of his favour to his people. It was more the praise of Cyrus to be God's shepherd than to be emperor of Persia. [3.] God makes what use he pleases of men, of mighty men, of those that act with the greatest freedom; and, when they think to do as they please, he can overrule them, and make them do as he pleases. Nay, in those very things wherein they are serving themselves, and look no further than that, God is serving his own purposes by them and making them to perform all his pleasure. Rich princes shall do what poor prophets have foretold.  <chapter eID="Isa.44"/> <div eID="gen16499" type="x-p"/>

entries.b2b5fbcea4f037d3027bf1f081db2904cdf97e60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9161"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 44</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.1-Isa.44.28">Is 44:1-28</reference>. Continuation of the Previous Chapter.</title> <div sID="gen15557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9161"/><hi type="bold">1-5. Yet--</hi>Though thou hast sinned, yet hear God's gracious promise as to thy deliverance.<div eID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15558" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chosen--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.41.8">Is 41:8</reference>). <div eID="gen15558" type="x-p"/>
entries.13aed915b756d67c60bb5600464e44a96053cecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9166"/><div sID="gen15574" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9166"/>6. Here follows an argument for Jehovah, as the only God, and against the idols, as vanity (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.4">Is 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Is 43:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.10-Isa.43.12">Is 43:10-12</reference>). <div eID="gen15574" type="x-p"/>
entries.e94c6c72a59d40901997fa8942290c4dfdfbcaea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9167"/><div sID="gen15575" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9167"/>7. Who but God can predict future events and declare also the order and time of each (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.22">Is 41:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.21">Is 45:21</reference>)?<div eID="gen15575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15576" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call--</hi>"openly proclaim" (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Is 40:6</reference>) things to come [Maurer]. Or, "call forth" the event; command that it happen (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.11">Is 46:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.15">48:15</reference>), [Barnes].<div eID="gen15576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15577" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set ... in order--</hi>There is no chance or confusion; all events occur in the order best fitted to subserve God's plans.<div eID="gen15577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for me--</hi>It is FOR God that all things exist and take place (<reference osisRef="Rev.4.11">Re 4:11</reference>). But Maurer translates, "Let him set it forth (<reference osisRef="Job.37.19">Job 37:19</reference>) to me."<div eID="gen15578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15579" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">since ... ancient people--</hi>I have given the Jews predictions of the future ever since I appointed them as My people in ancient times; therefore they were qualified to be His witnesses (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Is 44:8</reference>). As to their being God's "ancient (everlasting) people," see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.7-Deut.32.9">De 32:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>; the type of the redeemed Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen15579" type="x-p"/>
entries.af4bf17a9622c52ab8eddbfaa03f13973aea51f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9168"/><div sID="gen15580" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9168"/><hi type="bold">8. be afraid--</hi>literally, "be astounded," or "distracted with fear."<div eID="gen15580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from that time--</hi>namely, from the time that "I appointed the ancient people" (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Is 44:7</reference>). From the time of Abraham's call, his family were the depositories of the predictions of the Redeemer, whereas the promise of Cyrus was not heard of till Isaiah's time; therefore, the event to the prediction and accomplishment of which God appeals in proof of His sole Godhead, is the redemption of man by a descendant of Abraham, in whose person "the ancient people" was first formally "appointed." The deliverance of the Jews, by Cyrus, is mentioned afterwards only as an earnest of that greater mercy [Horsley].<div eID="gen15581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no God--</hi>Hebrew, tsur, "rock" (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.4">De 32:4</reference>); that is, a stronghold to take refuge in, and a solid foundation to build on. <div eID="gen15582" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b3acaef27ef0426b4650dd3eb51b74d55f2c574: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9169"/><div sID="gen15583" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9169"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Is 40:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">41:29</reference>).<div eID="gen15583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15584" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delectable things--</hi>the idols in which they take such pride and delight.<div eID="gen15584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not profit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hab.2.18">Ha 2:18</reference>).<div eID="gen15585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are their own witnesses--</hi>contrasted with, "Ye are My witnesses" (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Is 44:8</reference>). "They," that is, both the makers and the idols, are witnesses against themselves, for the idols palpably see and know nothing (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.4-Ps.115.8">Psa 115:4-8</reference>).<div eID="gen15586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15587" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they may be ashamed--</hi>the consequence deducible from the whole previous argument, not merely from the words immediately preceding, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Is 28:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.36.12">36:12</reference>. I say all this to show that they are doomed to perish with shame, which is their only fitting end. <div eID="gen15587" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3c54e840de224e1ab794d939d097232575c7634: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9170"/><div sID="gen15588" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9170"/><hi type="bold">10. Who ... ?--</hi>Sarcastic question: "How debased the man must be who forms a god!" It is a contradiction in terms. A made god, worshipped by its maker (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Co 8:4</reference>)! <div eID="gen15588" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3fca6cc5ae69d67714fa8d4a6dfd071fe312bd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9171"/><div sID="gen15589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9171"/><hi type="bold">11. his fellows--</hi>the associates of him who makes an idol; or of the idol (see <reference osisRef="Deut.7.26">De 7:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.8">Psa 115:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">Ho 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen15589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are of men--</hi>They are mortal men themselves; what better, then, can the idol be than its maker?<div eID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gathered together ... stand up--</hi>as in a court of justice, to try the issue between God and them (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.41.1">Is 41:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.21">Is 41:21</reference>).<div eID="gen15591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yet--</hi>wrongly inserted in English Version. The issue of the trial shall be, "they shall fear," &c. <div eID="gen15592" type="x-p"/>
entries.2771e19c1c3dbcdd6ab41bc56e9597769f572173: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9172"/><div sID="gen15593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9172"/><hi type="bold">12. tongs--</hi>rather, "prepareth (to be supplied) an axe," namely, with which to cut down the tree designed as the material of the idol. The "smith" (Hebrew, "workman in iron") here answers to the "carpenter" (Hebrew, "workman in wood"). "He worketh it (the axe, not the idol, which was wood, not metal) in the coals," &c. The axe was wrought, not cast. The smith makes the axe for the carpenter.<div eID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hungry ... drinketh no water--</hi>so eager is he to expedite his work while the iron is hot. If the god were worth anything, it would not let him grow "faint" with hunger and thirst. Williams, the missionary, states that the South Sea islanders when they make an idol abstain from food and drink. <div eID="gen15594" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfedf5407d6eb767e8c5424ddf48de2ad4c6f0cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9173"/><div sID="gen15595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9173"/>13. After the smith's work in preparing the instruments comes the carpenter's work in forming the idol.<div eID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rule--</hi>rather, "line" [Barnes].<div eID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15597" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with a line--</hi>rather, a "pencil," [Horsley]. Literally, "red ochre," which he uses to mark on the wood the outline of the figure [Lowth]. Or best, the stylus or graver, with which the incision of the outline is made [Gesenius].<div eID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">planes--</hi>rather, "chisels" or "carving tools," for a plane would not answer for carving.<div eID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">compass--</hi>from a Hebrew root, "to make a circle"; by it, symmetry of form is secured.<div eID="gen15599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15600" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">according to ... beauty of a man--</hi>irony. The highest idea the heathen could form of a god was one of a form like their own. Jerome says, "The more handsome the statue the more august the god was thought." The incarnation of the Son of God condescends to this anthropomorphic feeling so natural to man, but in such a way as to raise man's thoughts up to the infinite God who "is a spirit."<div eID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that it may remain in ... house--</hi>the only thing it was good for; it could not hear nor save (compare Wisdom 13:15). <div eID="gen15601" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a6b4dc7f91c25baa60850b74252346f66309373: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9174"/><div sID="gen15602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9174"/>14. Description of the material out of which the idol is formed.<div eID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cypress--</hi>rather, from Hebrew root, "to be hard," the holm oak," an evergreen abundant in Palestine [Gesenius].<div eID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strengtheneth--</hi>literally, "and he getteth strength to himself in the trees of the forest;" that is, he layeth in a great store of timber [Lowth]. Or, "chooseth," as "madest strong for thyself," that is, hast chosen (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Psa 80:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">17</reference>) [Gesenius]. But English Version gives a good sense: "strengtheneth"; that is, rears to maturity; a meaning suitable also to the context of <reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Psa 80:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">17</reference>, where Israel is compared to a vine planted by Jehovah [Maurer].<div eID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rain doth nourish it--</hi>Though the man planted the tree, yet he could not make it grow. In preparing to make an idol, he has to depend on the true God for rain from heaven (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jr 14:22</reference>). <div eID="gen15605" type="x-p"/>
entries.cdd145a23ba306ec9cc6fab54d47d65f37c1ea8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9175"/><div sID="gen15606" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9175"/>15. The same tree that furnishes the material for the god is in part used as fuel for a fire to cook his meals and warm himself!<div eID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15607" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thereto--</hi>rather, "he falleth down before them," that is, such images [Maurer]. <div eID="gen15607" type="x-p"/>
entries.caa856e2635495f5f58b32af2c2405e57c401e4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9176"/><div sID="gen15608" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9176"/><hi type="bold">16. part ... part--</hi>not distinct parts, but the same part of the wood (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.44.17">Is 44:17</reference>).<div eID="gen15608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eateth--</hi>that is, cooks so as to eat (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">Is 44:19</reference>).<div eID="gen15609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have seen--</hi>I feel its power. <div eID="gen15610" type="x-p"/>
entries.32f19f08189d3e425e9c18c48bf2dd7c8053509d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9177"/><div sID="gen15611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9177"/><hi type="bold">18. he, &c.--</hi>God hath given them over to judicial blindness; not His direct physical, but His providential agency in administering His moral government, is meant (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">10</reference>). "Shut," literally, "daubed," plastered up; it is an Eastern custom in some cases to seal up the eyes of offenders. <div eID="gen15611" type="x-p"/>
entries.298689d44ccbd64c02f7b20da9095084948e9e4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9178"/><div sID="gen15612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9178"/><hi type="bold">19. considereth--</hi>literally, "layeth it to heart," (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Is 42:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.11">Jr 12:11</reference>).<div eID="gen15612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15613" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abomination--</hi>the scriptural term for an idol, not merely abominable, but the essence of what is so, in the eyes of a jealous God (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1Ki 11:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.7">7</reference>). <div eID="gen15613" type="x-p"/>
entries.07a7dce7398e5a54ca6ffdfc8342a69a14fe79a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9179"/><div sID="gen15614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9179"/><hi type="bold">20. feedeth on ashes--</hi>figuratively, for the idolater delights in what is vain (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.14">Pr 15:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>). "Feedeth on wind." There is an allusion, perhaps, also, to the god being made of a tree, the half of which was reduced to ashes by fire (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.15-Isa.44.17">Is 44:15-17</reference>); the idol, it is implied, was no better, and could, and ought, to have been reduced to ashes like the other half.<div eID="gen15614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15615" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceived heart--</hi>The heart and will first go astray, then the intellect and life (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Ro 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.18">Ep 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen15615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lie in ... right hand--</hi>Is not my handiwork (the idol) a self-deceit? <div eID="gen15616" type="x-p"/>
entries.e43ef4f9c30f472641770d21073dba81c1cd14ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9180"/><div sID="gen15617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9180"/><hi type="bold">21. Remember--</hi>"Be not like the idolaters who consider not in their heart" (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">Is 44:19</reference>).<div eID="gen15617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15618" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these--</hi>things just said as to the folly of idol-worship.<div eID="gen15618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my servant--</hi>not like the idolaters, slaves to the stock of a tree (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">Is 44:19</reference>). See <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">Is 44:1</reference>, 2.<div eID="gen15619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15620" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... not ... forgotten of me--</hi>Therefore thou oughtest to "remember" Me. <div eID="gen15620" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac2c24cc0422ca94bc535450a877faedc9533ed4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9181"/><div sID="gen15621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9181"/><hi type="bold">22. blotted out--</hi>the debt of thy sin from the account-book in which it was entered (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">Ex 32:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.20.12">Re 20:12</reference>).<div eID="gen15621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a thick cloud--</hi>scattered away by the wind (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.12">Psa 103:12</reference>).<div eID="gen15622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a cloud--</hi>a descending gradation. Not only the "thick cloud" of the heavier "transgressions," but the "cloud" ("vapor" [Lowth], not so dense, but covering the sky as a mist) of the countless "sins." These latter, though not thought much of by man, need, as much as the former, to be cleared away by the Sun of righteousness; else they will be a mist separating us from heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Psa 19:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.7-1John.1.9">1Jo 1:7-9</reference>).<div eID="gen15623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">return ... for--</hi>The antecedent redemption is the ground of, and motive to, repentance. We do not repent in order that He may redeem us, but because He hath redeemed us (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Lu 24:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.18">Ac 3:18</reference>,<reference osisRef="Acts.3.19">19</reference>). He who believes in his being forgiven cannot but love (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.43">Lu 7:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.47">47</reference>). <div eID="gen15624" type="x-p"/>
entries.a74a6440106154ef366d28af1e311067cc26483e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9182"/><div sID="gen15625" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9182"/>23. Call to inanimate nature to praise God; for it also shall share in the coming deliverance from "the bondage of corruption" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen15625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">done it--</hi>effected redemption for both the literal and spiritual Israel.<div eID="gen15626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15627" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lower parts, &c.--</hi>antithetical to "heavens"; "mountains," "forest," and "tree," are the intermediate objects in a descending gradation (see <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Psa 96:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.96.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen15627" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d107efb446b4525bad6bbfcec24900d1ab03756: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9183"/><div sID="gen15628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9183"/>24-28. Confirmation of His promises to the Church and Israel, by various instances of His omnipotence; among these the restoration of the Jews by Cyrus.<div eID="gen15628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">alone--</hi>literally, "Who was with Me?" namely, when I did it; answering to "by Myself," in the parallel clause (compare similar phrases, <reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Ho 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.30">Joh 5:30</reference>) [Maurer]. <div eID="gen15629" type="x-p"/>

entries.d37d0bb69e5929ed5263ebb148161e8a97c89cd0: <div eID="gen28257" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28258" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28259" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28259" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28258" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28260" type="x-p"/> This chapter, besides promises of redemption, of the effusion of the Spirit, and success of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1-Isa.44.5">Isa 44:1-5</reference>, sets forth, in a very sublime manner, the supreme power and foreknowledge, and absolute eternity, of the one true God; and exposes the folly and absurdity of idolatry with admirable force and elegance, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6-Isa.44.20">Isa 44:6-20</reference>.
