And to show that the knowledge of future events belongs only to Jehovah, whom all creation is again called to adore for the deliverance and reconciliation granted to his people, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.21-Isa.44.23">Isa 44:21-23</reference>, the prophet concludes with setting in a very strong point of view the absolute impotence of every thing considered great and insurmountable in the sight of men, when standing in the way of the Divine counsel; and mentions the future deliverer of the Jewish nation expressly by name, nearly two hundred years before his birth, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24-Isa.44.28">Isa 44:24-28</reference>.
entries.56a0d12fc31922683fa31b2a73991399f51ff17c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28275" type="x-p"/> Jesurun - Jeshurun means Israel. This name was given to that people by Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.33.26">Deu 33:26</reference>. The most probable account of it seems to be that in which the Jewish commentators agree; namely, that it is derived from ישר yashar, and signifies upright. In the same manner, Israel, as a people, is called משלם meshullam, perfect, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.19">Isa 42:19</reference>, They were taught of God, and abundantly furnished with the means of rectitude and perfection in his service and worship. Grotius thinks that ישרון yeshurun is a diminutive of ישראל yishrael, Israel; expressing peculiar fondness and affection; Ισραηλιδιον, O little Israel.
entries.16124df6f673fc3d5bb5199fc683947974e08bb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen28275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28276" type="x-p"/> They shall spring up as among the grass "They shall spring up as the grass among the waters" - בבין חציר bebeyn chatsir, "They shall spring up to the midst of, or rather, in among, the grass. "This cannot be right: eleven MSS., and thirteen editions, have כבין kebeyn, or כבן keben. Twenty-four MSS. read it without the י yod, בבן beben, in the son of the grass; and so reads the Chaldee; בבן beben, in the son of the grass. <div eID="gen28276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28277" type="x-p"/> Twenty-four MSS. of Dr. Kennicott's, thirty-three of De Rossi's, and one of my own, with six editions, have this reading. The Syriac, מבין mibbeyn. The true reading is in all probability כבין kebeyn; and the word מים mayim, which should have followed it, is lost out of the text: but it is happily supplied by the Septuagint, ὡς ανα μεσον ὑδατος, as among the water "In every place where there is water, there is always grass; for water makes every thing grow in the east." Sir John Chardin's note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.5">1Kgs 17:5</reference>. Harmer's Observations 1:64.
entries.84502c695c90b8903a0d00f50c5cd2da0f66702b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen28277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28278" type="x-p"/> Shall call himself "Shall be called" - Passive, יקרא yikkare; κληθησεται, Symmachus. <div eID="gen28278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28279" type="x-p"/> Another shall subscribe with his hand unto the Lord "This shall inscribe his hand to Jehovah" - Και ἑτερος επιγραψει χειρι (χειρα, Ag., Sym.) αυτου, Του Θεου ειμι· "And another shall write upon his hand, I belong to God." - Sept. They seem to have read here, as before, ליהוה אני laihovah ani, I belong to Jehovah. But the repetition of the same phrase without any variation is not elegant. However, they seem to have understood it rightly, as an allusion to the marks, which were made by punctures rendered indelible, by fire or by staining, upon the hand or some other part of the body, signifying the state or character of the person, and to whom he belonged. The slave was marked with the name of his master, the soldier, of his commander; the idolater, with the name or ensign of his god: Στιγματα επιγραφομενα δια των στρατευομενων εν ταις χερσιν· "Punctural inscriptions made by the soldiers on their hands." Aetius apud Turnebum Advers. <reference osisRef="Isa.24.12">Isa 24:12</reference>. Victuris in cute punctis milites scripti et matriculis inserti jurare solent. "The soldiers having indelible inscriptions on their skin, and inserted in the muster-rolls, are accustomed to make oath." Vigetius, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>. And the Christians seem to have imitated this practice, by what Procopius says on this place of Isaiah: Το δε ΤΗ ΧΕΙΡΙ, δια το στιζειν ισως πολλους επι καρπων, η βραχιονων, η του σταυρου σημειον, η την Χριστου προσηγοριαν. "Because many marked their wrists, or their arms, with the sign of the cross, or with the name of Christ." See <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Rev 20:4</reference>; Spencer, De Leg. Hebr. lib. ii., cap. 20.
entries.a675d7bceeacef6f259b4e9e86b6b44b21d27f8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28280" type="x-p"/> Let them show unto them "Let them declare unto us" - For למו lamo, unto them, the Chaldee reads לנו lanu, unto us The Septuagint read לכם lachem, unto you; which is preferable to the reading of the text. But למו lamo, and לנו lanu, are frequently mistaken one for the other, see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.29">Isa 10:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.80.7">Psa 80:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.64.6">Psa 64:6</reference>.
entries.b9af5be727976ff1e8ea32f6014be1e2a7158402: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28281" type="x-p"/> Fear ye not - תרהו - to tirehu never occurs. Perhaps it should be תיראו tireu, fear ye. Two MSS. read תירהו tirehu, and one of mine תהרו taharu.
entries.86c8927d723717917a248c2dc5a835ecea530c28: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28282" type="x-p"/> That they may be ashamed. Who hath formed a god "That every one may be ashamed, that he hath formed a god" - The Bodleian MS., one of the first extant for its antiquity and authority, instead of מי mi, at the beginning of the tenth verse, has כי ki, which greatly clears up the construction of a very obscure passage. Doederlein approves of this reading. The Septuagint likewise closely connect in construction the end of <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference> with the beginning of <reference osisRef="Isa.44.10">Isa 44:10</reference>; and wholly omit the interrogative מי mi, which embarrasses the sentence: Αισχυνθησονται οἱ πλασσοντες Θεον, και γλυφοντες παντες ανωφελη· "But they shall be confounded that make a god; and they who engrave unprofitable things;" agreeably to the reading of the MS. above mentioned.
entries.fb5779540f8104c193eaf477875fa75d4b83f079: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28283" type="x-p"/> His fellows - חבריו chaberaiv: but עבדיו abadaiv, his servants or worshippers, is the reading of one of De Rossi's MSS., and of the Chaldee. <div eID="gen28283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28284" type="x-p"/> And the workmen, they are of men "Even the workmen themselves shall blush" - I do not know that any one has ever yet interpreted these words to any tolerably good sense: וחרשים המה מאדם vecharashim hemmah meadam. The Vulgate and our translators, have rendered them very fairly, as they are written and pointed in the text: Fabri enim sunt ex hominibus. "And the workmen they are of men." Out of which the commentators have not been able to extract any thing worthy of the prophet. I have given another explanation of the place; agreeable enough to the context, if it can be deduced from the words themselves. I presume that אדם adam, rubuit, may signify erubuit, to be red through shame, as well as from any other cause; though I cannot produce any example of it in that particular sense; and the word in the text I would point מאדם meoddam; or if any one should object to the irregularity of the number, I would read מאדמים meoddamim. But I rather think that the irregularity of the construction has been the cause of the obscurity, and has given occasion to the mistaken punctuation. The singular is sometimes put for the plural. See <reference osisRef="Psa.68.31">Psa 68:31</reference>; and the participle for the future tense, see <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa 40:11</reference>. - L.
entries.c679972727e7b84718de6864769ed7a7ab7ea005: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28285" type="x-p"/> The smith with the tongs, etc. "The smith cutteth off a portion of iron" - מעצד meatstsed, Participium Pihel of עצד atsad, to cut; still used in that sense in the Arabic. See Simonis Lex. Hebrews The Septuagint and Syriac take the word in this form: but they render it sharpeneth the iron. See Castell. Lex. in voce. <div eID="gen28285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28286" type="x-p"/> The sacred writers are generally large and eloquent upon the subject of idolatry; they treat it with great severity, and set forth the absurdity of it in the strongest light. But this passage of Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12-Isa.44.20">Isa 44:12-20</reference>, far exceeds any thing that ever was written upon the subject, in force of argument, energy of expression, and elegance of composition. One or two of the apocryphal writers have attempted to imitate the prophet, but with very ill success; Wisd. 13:11-19; 15:7, etc.; Baruch 6, NAB (editor's note: some translations treat this as Letter to Jeremiah), especially the latter, who, injudiciously dilating his matter, and introducing a number of minute circumstances, has very much weakened the force and effect of his invective. On the contrary a heathen author, in the ludicrous way, has, in a line or two, given idolatry one of the severest strokes it ever received: - <div eID="gen28286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28287" type="x-p"/> Olim truncus eram ficulnus, inutile lignum, <div eID="gen28287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28288" type="x-p"/> Cum faber incertus, scamnum faceretne <div eID="gen28288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28289" type="x-p"/> Priapum, Maluit esse Deum. Deus inde ego. <div eID="gen28289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28290" type="x-p"/> Horat. Satyr, lib. 1. sat. viii. "Formerly I was the stump of a fig tree, a useless log; when the carpenter, after hesitating whether to make me a god or a stool, at last determined to make me a god. Thus I became a god!" <div eID="gen28290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28291" type="x-p"/> From the tenth to the seventeenth verse, a most beautiful strain of irony is carried on against idolatry. And we may naturally think that every idolater, who either read or heard it, must have been for ever ashamed of his own devices. - L.
entries.044b9792809b1b876c7cdfd72a6f6ae508251feb: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28292" type="x-p"/> He heweth him down "He heweth down" - For לכרת lichroth, the Septuagint and Vulgate read כרת carath or יכרת yichroth.
entries.91816611f0ee9d23bc782b46079f9eebb2729e6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28293" type="x-p"/> With part "And with part" - Twenty-three MSS., the Septuagint, and Vulgate add the conjunction ו vau, and ועל veal.
entries.4b0ee4655117b6db29c35ace3b92f7109f934183: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen28293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28294" type="x-p"/> He falleth down unto it - There were four forms of adoration used among the Hebrews: <div eID="gen28294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28295" type="x-p"/> 1. השתחוה Hishtachavah, The prostration of the whole body. <div eID="gen28295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28296" type="x-p"/> 2. קדד Kadad, The bowing of the head. <div eID="gen28296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28297" type="x-p"/> 3. כרע Cara, The bending of the upper part of the body down to the knees. <div eID="gen28297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28298" type="x-p"/> 4. ברך Barach, Bowing the knee, or kneeling. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.49.23">Isa 49:23</reference> (note).
entries.681f6e95e418824d886d0774ccc4efc8a222dbc4: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen28298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28299" type="x-p"/> He hath shut their eyes "Their eyes are closed up" - The Septuagint, Chaldee, and Vulyate, for טח tach, read טחו tachu. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>.  <chapter eID="Isa.44"/> <div eID="gen28299" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c8ebc692bb5c3803de2df21322f4babcc05dacf: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen28260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28261" type="x-p"/> He feedeth on ashes - He feedeth on that which affordeth no nourishment; a proverbial expression for using ineffectual means, and bestowing labor to no purpose. In the same sense Hosea says, "Ephraim feedeth on wind." <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos 12:1</reference>.
entries.7faf240d79d7ae822b6653e742455e21b6a9d82c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen28261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28262" type="x-p"/> I have blotted out, as a thick cloud, thy transgressions, and, as a cloud, thy sins "I have made thy transgressions vanish away like a cloud, and thy sins like a vapor" - Longinus admired the sublimity of the sentiment, as well as the harmony of the numbers, in the following sentence of Demosthenes: Τουτο το ψηφισμα τον τοτε τῃ πολει τερισταντα κινδυνον παρελθειν εποιησεν ὡσπερ νεφος. "This decree made the danger then hanging over the city pass away like a cloud." Probably Isaiah alludes here to the smoke rising up from the sin-offering, dispersed speedily by the wind. and rendered invisible. He who offered his sacriflce aright was as sure that the sin for which he offered it was blotted out, as that the smoke of the sacrifice was dispersed by the wind, and was no longer discernible.
entries.e60e718d6af7a7bf49bc92a9e2f734975992f623: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen28262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28263" type="x-p"/> By myself - Thirteen MSS., six ancient, confirm the reading of the Keri, מאתי meittai.
entries.1916e7a4d7d00ba5810e61ec11bf528758b3b5fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen28263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28264" type="x-p"/> That saith to the deep, Be dry "Who saith to the deep, Be thou wasted" - Cyrus took Babylon by laying the bed of the Euphrates dry, and leading his army into the city by night through the empty channel of the river. This remarkable circumstance, in which the event so exactly corresponded with the prophecy, was also noted by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jer 50:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">Jer 51:36</reference>. "A drought shall be upon her waters, and they shall be dried up: - <div eID="gen28264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28265" type="x-p"/> I will lay her sea dry <div eID="gen28265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28266" type="x-p"/> And I will scorch up her springs." <div eID="gen28266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28267" type="x-p"/> It is proper here to give some account of the means and method lay which the stratagem of Cyrus was effected. <div eID="gen28267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28268" type="x-p"/> The Euphrates in the middle of the summer, from the melting of the snows on the mountains of Armenia, like the Nile, overflows the country. In order to diminish the inundation, and to carry off the waters, two canals were made by Nebuchadnezzar a hundred miles above the city; the first on the eastern side called Naharmalca, or the Royal River, by which the Euphrates was let into the Tigris; the other on the western side, called Pallacopas, or Naharaga, (נהר אגם nahar agam, The river of the pool), by which the redundant waters were carried into a vast lake, forty miles square, contrived, not only to lessen the inundation, but for a reservoir, with sluices, to water the barren country on the Arabian side. Cyrus, by turning the whole river into the lake by the Pallacopas, laid the channel, where it ran through the city, almost dry; so that his army entered it, both above and below, by the bed of the river, the water not reaching above the middle of the thigh. By the great quantity-of water let into the lake, the sluices and dams were destroyed; and being never repaired afterwards, the waters spread over the whole country below, and reduced it to a morass, in which the river is lost. Ingens modo et navigabilis, inde tenuis rivus, despectus emoritur; et nusquam manifesto exitit effluit, ut alii omnes, sed deficit. "And thus a navigable river has been totally lost, it having no exit from this morass. No wonder then that the geographical face of this country is completely changed;" Mela <reference osisRef="Jer.3.8">Jer 3:8</reference>; Herod. 1:186, 190; Xenophon, Cyrop. vii.; Arrian vii.
entries.df748ddf65ce9fc60c30f57dcd3d6099d8b006f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen28268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28269" type="x-p"/> That saith of Cyrus, He is my shepherd "Who saith to Cyrus, Thou art my shepherd" - Pastor meus es; Vulg. The true reading seems to be רעי אתה roi attah; the word אתה attah, has probably been dropped out of the text. The same word is lost out of the text, <reference osisRef="Psa.119.57">Psa 119:57</reference>. It is supplied in the Septuagint by the word ει, thou art. <div eID="gen28269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28270" type="x-p"/> Saying to Jerusalem - For ולאמר velemor, the Septuagint and Vulgate read האומר haomer. <div eID="gen28270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28271" type="x-p"/> And to the temple - ולהיכל uleheychal, as לירושלם lirushalayim, before; the preposition is necessary, and the Vulgate seems to read so. - Houbigant. <div eID="gen28271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28272" type="x-p"/> That saith of Cyrus, He is, or thou art, my shepherd - Saying to Jerusalem, "Thou shalt be built;" and to the Temple, "Thy foundation shall be laid." - There is a remarkable beauty and propriety in this verse. <div eID="gen28272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28273" type="x-p"/> 1. Cyrus is called God's shepherd. Shepherd was an epithet which Cyrus took to himself; and what he gave to all good kings. <div eID="gen28273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28274" type="x-p"/> 2. This Cyrus should say to the temple: "Thy foundation shall be laid." Not - thou shalt be built. The fact is, only the foundation was laid in the days of Cyrus, the Ammonites having prevented the building; nor was it resumed till the second year of Darius, one of his successors. There is often a precision in the expressions of the prophets which is as honorable to truth, as it is unnoticed by careless readers.

entries.04b0f14709284f82ae0b0f648a262034d79a3f4a: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1-Isa.44.4">Isa 44:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen13401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13402" type="x-p"/> The prophet cannot bear to dwell any longer upon this dark picture of their state of punishment; and light of the promise breaks through again, and in this third field of the fourth prophecy in all the more intensive form. <hi type="italic">“And now hear, O Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen. Thus saith Jehovah, thy Creator, and thy Former from the womb, who cometh to thy help; Fear not, my servant Jacob; and Jeshurun, whom I have chosen! For I will pour out water upon thirsty ones, and brooks upon the dry ground; will pour out my Spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine after-growth; and they shoot up among the grass, as willows by flowing waters.”</hi> In contrast with the cheerem, i.e., the setting apart for destruction, there is here presented the promise of the pouring out of the Spirit and of blessing; and in contrast with the <hi type="italic">giddūphı̄m</hi>, the promise of general eagerness to come and honour Israel and its God (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference>). The epithets by which Jehovah designates Himself, and those applied to Israel in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">Isa 44:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.2">Isa 44:2</reference>, make the claim to love all the more urgent and emphatic. The accent which connects מבּטן ויצרך, so as to make יעזרך by itself an attributive clause like בו בּחרתּי, is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa 49:5</reference> : Israel as a nation and all the individuals within it are, as the chosen servant of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.1">Isa 49:1</reference>), the direct formation of Jehovah Himself from the remotest point of their history. In <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa 44:26</reference>, <hi type="italic">Jeshurun</hi> is used interchangeably with Jacob. This word occurs in three other passages (viz., <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.5">Deu 33:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.26">Deu 33:26</reference>), and is always written with <hi type="italic">kibbutz</hi>, just as it is here. The rendering ̓Ισραελίσκος in <hi type="italic">Gr. Ven.</hi> is founded upon the supposition that the word is equivalent to ישׂרלוּן - a strange contraction, which is inadmissible, if only on account of the substitution of שׁ for שׂ. The שׁ points back to ישׁר, to be straight or even; hence A. S. Th. εὐθύσς (elsewhere εὐθύτατος), Jerome <hi type="italic">rectissimus</hi> (though in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.15">Deu 32:15</reference> he renders it, after the lxx, <hi type="italic">dilectus</hi>). It is an offshoot of ישׁר = ישׁר (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.21">Psa 25:21</reference>), like זבלוּן, ידתוּן from זבל, ידת; and <hi type="italic">ūn</hi> (= <hi type="italic">ōn</hi>) does not stamp it as a diminutive (for אישׁון, which Kamphausen adduces in opposition to Hengstenberg and Volck, does not stand in the same relation to אישׁ as mannikin to man, but rather as the image of a man to a man himself; compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">insân</hi>). We must not render it therefore as an affectionate diminutive, as Gesenius does, the more especially as Jehovah, though speaking in loving terms, does not adopt the language of a lover. The relation of <hi type="italic">Jeshurun</hi> to ישׁר is rather the same as that of שׁלמה to שׁלום, so that the real meaning is “gentleman,” or one of gentlemanly or honourable mind, though this need not appear in the translation, since the very nature of a proper name would obliterate it. In <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference>, the blessings to be expected are assigned as the reason for the exhortation to be of good cheer. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference></hi> water is promised in the midst of drought, and in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference></hi> the Spirit and blessing of God, just as in Joel the promise of rain is first of all placed in contrast with drought; and this is followed by the promise of the far surpassing antitype, namely, the outpouring of the Spirit. There is nothing at variance with this in the fact that we have not the form צמאה in the place of צמא fo e (according to the analogy of עיפה ארץ, ציּה, נלאה, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.10">Psa 68:10</reference>). By צמא) we understand the inhabitants of the land who are thirsting for rain, and by <hi type="italic">yabbâshâh</hi> the parched land itself. Further on, however, an express distinction is made between the abundance of water in the land and the prosperous growth of the nation planted by the side of water-brooks (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>). We must not regard <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference></hi>, therefore, as a figure, and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference></hi> as the explanation, or turn <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa 44:3</reference></hi> into a simile introduced in the form of a protasis, although unquestionably water and mountain streams are made the symbol, or rather the anagogical type, of spiritual blessings coming down from above in the form of heavenly gifts, by a gradual ascent from מים and נוזלים (from נזל, to trickle downwards, Sol 4:15, <reference osisRef="Jer.18.14">Jer 18:14</reference>) to ה רוּח and ה בּרכת (בּרכּת). When these natural and spiritual waters flow down upon the people, once more restored to their home, they spring up among (בּבין only met with here, lxx and Targum כּבין) the grass, like willows by water-brooks. <div eID="gen13402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13403" type="x-p"/> The willows<note placement="foot">“The <hi type="italic">garab</hi>,” says Wetzstein, “was only met with by me in one locality, or, at any rate, I only noticed it once, namely in the <hi type="italic">Wady</hi> <hi type="italic">So'êb</hi>, near to a ford of the river which is called the <hi type="italic">Hôd</hi> ford, from the <hi type="italic">chirbet</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Hôd</hi>, a miserable ruin not far off. It is half an hour to the west of <hi type="italic">Nimrin</hi> (<hi type="italic">Nimrim</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.15.6">Isa 15:6</reference>), or, speaking more exactly, half an hour above (i.e., to the east of) <hi type="italic">Zafât</hi> <hi type="italic">Nimriin</hi>, an antique road on the northern bank of the river, hewn in a precipitous wall of rock, like the ladder of Tyre. I travelled through the valley in June 1860, and find the following entry in my diary: 'At length the ravine opened up into a broader valley, so that we could get down to the clear, copious, and rapid stream, and were able to cross it. Being exhausted by the heat, we lay down near the ford among the oleanders, which the mass of flowers covered with a rosy glow. The reed grows here to an unusual height, as in the <hi type="italic">Wady</hi> <hi type="italic">Yarmûk</hi>, and willows (<hi type="italic">zafzaf</hi>) and <hi type="italic">garab </hi>are mingled together, and form many-branched trees of three or four fathoms in height. The vegetation, which is fresh and luxuriant by the water-side, is scorched up with the heat in the valley within as little as ten paces from the banks of the stream. The farthest off is the <hi type="italic">'osar</hi> plant, with its thick, juicy, dark green stalks and leaves, and its apple-like fruit, which is of the same colour, and therefore not yet ripe. The <hi type="italic">garab</hi> tree has already done flowering. The leaves of this tree stand quite close around the stem, as in the case of the <hi type="italic">Sindiana</hi> (the Syrian oak), and, like the leaves of the latter, are fringed with little thorns; but, like the willow, it is a water plant, and our companions <hi type="italic">Abdallah</hi> and <hi type="italic">Nasrallah</hi> assured us that it was only met with near flowing water and in hot lowlands. Its bunches of flowers are at the points of the slender branches, and assume an umbelliferous form. This is the ערב of the Bible.' Consequently the <hi type="italic">garab</hi> (or (as <hi type="italic">nom. unitatis</hi>) the garaba cannot be regarded as a species of willow; and Winer’s assumption (<hi type="italic">Real-Wörterbuch, s.v. Weiden</hi>), that the weeping willow is intended at any rate in <reference osisRef="Ps.137.2">Psa 137:2</reference>, is an error. In Arabic the weeping willow is always called <hi type="italic">shafshaf</hi> <hi type="italic">mustachi</hi> (the drooping tree). At the same time, we may render ערבים 'willows,' since the <hi type="italic">garab</hi> loves running water as well as the willow, and apparently they seek one another’s society; it is quite enough that the difference should be clearly pointed out in the commentary. The reason why the <hi type="italic">garab</hi> did not find its way into my herbarium was the following. On my arrival in Salt, I received the first intelligence of the commencement of the slaughter of the Christians on Antilibanus, and heard the report, which was then commonly believed, that a command had been sent from Constantinople to exterminate Christianity from Syria. This alarming report compelled me to inquire into the actual state of affairs; therefore, leaving my luggage and some of my companions behind, I set off with all speed to Jerusalem, where I hoped to obtain reliable information, accompanied by Herr Dörgen, my kavas, and two natives, viz., <hi type="italic">Abdallah</hi> the smith, from Salt, and <hi type="italic">Nasrallah</hi> the smith, from <hi type="italic">Ain Genna</hi>. For a ride like this, which did not form part of the original plan of my journey, everything but weapons, even a herbarium, would have been in the way. Still there are small caravans going every week between Salt and Jerusalem, and they must always cross the <hi type="italic">Hôd</hi> ford, so that it would be easy to get a twig of the <hi type="italic">garab</hi>. So far as I remember, the remains of the blossom were of a dirty white colour.” (Compare p. 213, where we have taken <hi type="italic">nachal hâ‛ărâbhı̄m</hi>, according to the meaning of the words, as a synonym of <hi type="italic">Wady Sufsaf</hi>, or, more correctly, <hi type="italic">Safsâf</hi>. From the description given above, the <hi type="italic">garab</hi> is a kind of <hi type="italic">viburnum</hi> with indented leaves. This tree, which is of moderate height, is found by the side of streams along with the willow. According to Sprengel (<hi type="italic">Gesch. der Botanik</hi>. i. 25), the <hi type="italic">safsâf</hi> is the <hi type="italic">salix subserrata</hi> of Wildenow).</note> are the nation, which has hitherto resembled withered plants in a barren soil, but is now restored to all the bloom of youth through the Spirit and blessing of God. The grass stands for the land, which resembles a green luxuriant plain; and the water-brooks represent the abundant supply of living waters, which promote the prosperity of the land and its inhabitants.
entries.2d8fc8e62dba325997da35b0a22d76bafd401f76: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.5">Isa 44:5</reference> <div eID="gen13403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13404" type="x-p"/> When Jehovah has thus acknowledged His people once more, the heathen, to whose <hi type="italic">giddūphı̄m</hi> (blasphemies) Israel has hitherto been given up, will count it the greatest honour to belong to Jehovah and His people. <hi type="italic">“One will say, I belong to Jehovah; and a second will solemnly name the name of Jacob; and a third will inscribe himself to Jehovah, and name the name of Israel with honour.”</hi> The threefold <hi type="italic">zeh</hi> refers to the heathen, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Psa 87:4</reference>-5. One will declare himself to belong to Jehovah; another will call with the name of Jacob, i.e., (according to the analogy of the phrase ה בשׁם קרא) make it the medium and object of solemn exclamation; a third will write with his hand (ידו, an acc. of more precise definition, like חמה in <reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>, and זביחך in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.23">Isa 43:23</reference>), “To Jehovah,” thereby attesting that he desires to belong to Jehovah, and Jehovah alone. This is the explanation given by Gesenius, Hahn, and others; whereas Hitzig and Knobel follow the lxx in the rendering, “he will write upon his hand '<hi type="italic">‛layehōvâh</hi>,' i.e., mark the name of Jehovah upon it.” But apart from the fact that <hi type="italic">kâthabh</hi>, with an accusative of the writing materials, would be unprecedented (the construction required would be על־ידו), this view is overthrown by the fact that tatooing was prohibited by the Israelitish law (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.28">Lev 19:28</reference>; compare the mark of the beast in <reference osisRef="Rev.13.16">Rev 13:16</reference>). בשׁם קרא is interchanged with בסם כּנּה, to surname, or entitle (the Syriac and Arabic are the same; compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">kunye</hi>, the name given to a man as the father of such and such a person, e.g., <hi type="italic">Abu-Muhammed</hi>, rhetorically called metonymy). The name <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> becomes a name or title of honour among the heathen. This concludes the fourth prophecy, which opens out into three distinct fields. With ועתּה in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.1">Isa 44:1</reference> it began to approach the close, just as the third did in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Isa 43:1</reference> -a well-rounded whole, which leaves nothing wanting.
entries.845be6b17b6f13fffd763d753904bccccbdbb81d: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6-Isa.44.7">Isa 44:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen13404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13405" type="x-p"/> A new pledge of redemption is given, and a fresh exhortation to trust in Jehovah; the wretchedness of the idols and their worshippers being pointed out, in contrast with Jehovah, the only speaking and acting God. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.6">Isa 44:6</reference> <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah the King of Israel, and its Redeemer, Jehovah of hosts; I am first, and I last; and beside me there is no God.”</hi> The fact that His deity, which rules over not only the natural world, but history as well, is thus without equal and above all time, is now proved by Him from the fact that He alone manifests Himself as God, and that by the utterance of prophecy. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.7">Isa 44:7</reference> <hi type="italic">“And who preaches as I do? Let him make it known, and show it to me; since I founded the people of ancient time! And future things, and what is approaching, let them only make known.”</hi> Jehovah shows Himself as the God of prophecy since the time that He founded עם־עולם (יקרא refers to the continued preaching of prophecy). <hi type="italic">‛Am‛ōlâm</hi> is the epithet applied in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Eze 26:20</reference> to the people of the dead, who are sleeping the long sleep of the grave; and here it does not refer to Israel, which could neither be called an “eternal” nation, nor a people of the olden time, and which would have been more directly named; but according to <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Isa 40:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>, where <hi type="italic">‛am</hi> signifies the human race, and Job 22:15., where <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi> is the time of the old world before the flood, it signifies humanity as existing from the very earliest times. The prophecies of Jehovah reach back even to the history of paradise. The parenthetical clause, “Let him speak it out, and tell it me,” is like the apodosis of a hypothetical protasis: “if any one thinks that he can stand by my side.” The challenge points to earlier prophecies; with ואתיּות it takes a turn to what is future, אתיות itself denoting what is absolutely future, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.41.23">Isa 41:23</reference>, and תּבאנה אשׁר what is about to be realized immediately; <hi type="italic">lâmō</hi> is an ethical dative.
entries.739a93fd1a8f14153e6d6438edaca2d07234cb0e: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Isa 44:8</reference> <div eID="gen13405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13406" type="x-p"/> Of course, none of the heathen gods could in any way answer to the challenge. So much the more confident might Israel be, seeing that it had quite another God. <hi type="italic">“Despair ye not, neither tremble: have not I told thee long ago, and made known, and ye are my witnesses: is there a God beside me? And nowhere a rock; I know of none.”</hi> The Jewish lexicographers derive תּרהוּ (with the first syllable closed) from רהה (רה); whereas modern lexicographers prefer some of them to read תּרהוּ, <hi type="italic">tı̄rehū</hi>, from ירהּ (Ges., Knobel), and others תּיראוּ (Ewald). But the possibility of there being a verb רהה, to tremble or fear, cannot for a moment be doubted when we think of such words as ירא, ירע, compare also Arab. <hi type="italic">r'h</hi> (applied to water moving to and fro). It was not of the heathen deities that they were directed not to be afraid, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.5">Jer 10:5</reference>, but rather the great catastrophe coming upon the nations, of which Cyrus was the instrument. In the midst of this, when one nation after another would be overthrown, and its tutelar gods would prove to be worthless, Israel would have nothing to fear, since its God, who was no dumb idol, had foretold all this, and that indeed long ago (מאז, cf., מראשׁ, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Isa 41:26</reference>), as they themselves must bear witness. Prophecies before the captivity had foretold the conquest of Babylon by Medes and Elamites, and the deliverance of Israel from the Babylonian bondage; and even these prophecies themselves were like a spirit’s voice from the far distant past, consoling the people of the captivity beforehand, and serving to support their faith. On the ground of such well-known self-manifestations, Jehovah could well ask, <hi type="italic">“Is there a God beside me?”</hi> - a virtual denial in the form of an interrogation, to which the categorical denial, “There is no rock (i.e., no ground of trust, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Isa 26:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.10">Isa 17:10</reference>), I know of none (beside me),” is attached.
entries.919d6d82b307d39eed0b144b94daec0f526360a7: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9-Isa.44.11">Isa 44:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen13406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13407" type="x-p"/> The heathen gods are so far from being a ground of trust, that all who trust in them must discover with alarm how they have deceived themselves. <hi type="italic">“The makers of idols, they are all desolation, and their bosom-children worthless; and those who bear witness for them see nothing and know nothing, that they may be put to shame. Who hath formed the god, and cast the idol to no profit? Behold, all its followers will be put to shame; and the workmen are men: let them all assemble together, draw near, be alarmed, be all put to shame together.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">chămūdı̄m</hi> (favourites) of the makers of idols are the false gods, for whose favour they sue with such earnestness. If we retain the word המּה, which is pointed as critically suspicious, and therefore is not accentuated, the explanation might possibly be, “Their witnesses (i.e., witnesses against themselves) are they (the idols): they see not, and are without consciousness, that they (those who trust in them) may be put to shame.” In any case, the subject to <hi type="italic">yēbhōshū</hi> (shall be put to shame) is the worshippers of idols. If we erase המה, (עדיהם will be those who come forward as witnesses for the idols. This makes the words easier and less ambiguous. At the same time, the Septuagint retains the word (καὶ μάρτυρες αὐτῶν εἰσίν). As “not seeing” here signifies to be blind, so “not knowing” is also to be understood as a self-contained expression, meaning to be irrational, just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.20">Isa 45:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Isa 56:10</reference> (in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>, on the other hand, we have taken it in a different sense). למען implies that the will of the sinner in his sin has also destruction for its object; and this is not something added to the sin, but growing out of it. The question in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.10">Isa 44:10</reference> summons the maker of idols for the purpose of announcing his fate, and in הועיל לבלתּי (to no profit) this announcement is already contained. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.11">Isa 44:11</reference> is simply a development of this expression, “to no profit.” יצר, like נטע in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.14">Isa 44:14</reference>, is contrary to the rhythmical law <hi type="italic">milra</hi> which prevails elsewhere. חבריו (its followers) are not the fellow-workmen of the maker of idols (inasmuch as in that case the maker himself would be left without any share in the threat), but the associates (i.e., followers) of the idols (Hos 4:17; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.20">1Co 10:20</reference>). It is a pernicious work that they have thus had done for them. And what of the makers themselves? They are numbered among the men. So that they who ought to know that they are made by God, become makers of gods themselves. What an absurdity! Let them crowd together, the whole guild of god-makers, and draw near to speak to the works they have made. All their eyes will soon be opened with amazement and alarm.
entries.b86411f32359198830e0f0061a220c34b06e5a1a: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12-Isa.44.13">Isa 44:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen13407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13408" type="x-p"/> The prophet now conducts us into the workshops. <hi type="italic">“The iron-smith has a chisel, and works with red-hot coals, and shapes it with hammers, and works it with his powerful arm. He gets hungry thereby, and his strength fails; if he drink no water, he becomes exhausted. The carpenter draws the line, marks it with the pencil, carries it out with planes, and makes a drawing of it with the compass, and carries it out like the figure of a man, like the beauty of a man, which may dwell in the house.”</hi> The two words <hi type="italic">chârash barzel</hi> are connected together in the sense of <hi type="italic">faber ferrarius</hi>, as we may see from the expression <hi type="italic">chârash</hi> <hi type="italic">‛ētsı̄m</hi> (the carpenter, <hi type="italic">faber lignarius</hi>), which follows in Isa 44:13. <hi type="italic">Chârash</hi> is the construct of <hi type="italic">chârâsh</hi> (= <hi type="italic">charrâsh</hi>), as in Exo 28:11. The second <hi type="italic">kametz</hi> of this form of noun does indeed admit of contraction, but only to the extent of a full short vowel; consequently the construct of the plural is not חרשׁי, but חרשׁי (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.16">Isa 45:16</reference>, etc.). Hence <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12">Isa 44:12</reference> describes how the smith constructs an idol of iron, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.13">Isa 44:13</reference> how the carpenter makes one of wood. But the first clause, מעצד בּרזל חרשׁ, is enigmatical. In any case, מעצד is a smith’s tool of some kind (from עצד, related to חצד). And consequently Gesenius, Umbreit, and others, adopt the rendering, “the smith an axe, that does he work ... ;” but the further account of the origin of an idol says nothing at all about this axe, which the smith supplies to the carpenter, that he may hew out an idol with it. Hitzig renders it, “The smith, a hatchet does he work, and forms it (viz., into an idol);” but what a roundabout way! first to make a hatchet and then make it into an idol, which would look very slim when made. Knobel translates it, “As for the cutting-smith, he works it;” but this guild of cutting-smiths certainly belongs to Utopia. The best way to render the sentence intelligible, would be to supply לו: “The smith has (uses) the <hi type="italic">ma‛ătsâd</hi>.” But in all probability a word has dropped out; and the Septuagint rendering, ὅτι ὤξυνεν τέκτων σίδηρον σκεπάρνω εἰργάσατο κ.τ.λ, shows that the original reading of the text was מעצד ברזל חרס חדד, and that חדד got lost on account of its proximity to יחץ. The meaning therefore is, “The smith has sharpened, or sharpens (<hi type="italic">chiddēd</hi>, syn. <hi type="italic">shinnēn</hi>) the <hi type="italic">ma‛ătsâd</hi>,” possibly the chisel, to cut the iron upon the anvil; and works with red-hot coals, making the iron red-hot by blowing the fire. The piece of iron which he cuts off is the future idol, and this he shapes with hammers (יצרהוּ the future of יצר). And what of the carpenter? He stretches the line upon the block of wood, to measure the length and breadth of the idol; he marks it upon the wood with red-stone (<hi type="italic">sered</hi>, <hi type="italic">rubrica</hi>, used by carpenters), and works it with planes (<hi type="italic">maqtsu‛ōth</hi>, a feminine form of מקצוע, from קצע, to cut off, pare off, plane; compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">mikta‛</hi>), and with the compasses (<hi type="italic">mechūgâh</hi>, the tool used, <hi type="italic">lâchūg</hi>, i.e. for making a circle) he draws the outline of it, that is to say, in order that the different parts of the body may be in right proportion; and he constructs it in such a manner that it acquires the shape of a man, the beautiful appearance of a man, to be set up like a human inmate in either a temple or private house. The <hi type="italic">piel</hi> תּאר (תּאר), from which comes <hi type="italic">yetāărēhū</hi>, is varied here (according to Isaiah’s custom; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5">Isa 26:5</reference>) with the <hi type="italic">poel</hi>תּאר, which is to be understood as denoting the more exact configuration. The preterites indicate the work for which both smith and carpenter have made their preparations; the futures, the work in which they are engaged.
entries.876cf1b88787215ca7cc5f16640f21f83201c557: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.14-Isa.44.17">Isa 44:14-17</reference> <div eID="gen13408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13409" type="x-p"/> The prophet now traces the origin of the idols still further back. Their existence or non-existence ultimately depends upon whether it rains or not. <hi type="italic">“One prepares to cut down cedars, and takes holm and oak-tree, and chooses for himself among the trees of the forest. He has planted a fig, and the rain draws it up. And it serves the man for firing: he takes thereof, and warms himself; he also heats, and bakes bread; he also works it into a god, and prostrates himself; makes an idol of it, and falls down before it. The half of it he has burned in the fire: over the half of it he eats flesh, roasts a roast, and is satisfied; he also warms himself, and says, Hurrah, I am getting warm, I feel the heat. And the rest of it he makes into a god, into his idol, and says, Save me, for thou art my god.”</hi> The subject of the sentence is not the carpenter of the previous verse, but “any one.” ארזים apparently stands first, as indicating the species; and in the <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> and Midrash the trees named are really described as ארזים מיני. But <hi type="italic">tirzâh</hi> (from <hi type="italic">târaz</hi>, to be hard or firm) does not appear to be a coniferous tree; and the connection with <hi type="italic">'allōn</hi>, the oak, is favourable to the rendering ἀγριοβάλανος (lxx, A. Th.), <hi type="italic">ilex</hi> (Vulg.). On <hi type="italic">'immēts</hi>, to choose, see Isa 41:10. ארן (with <hi type="italic">Nun minusculum</hi>), plur. ארונים (<hi type="italic">b.</hi> <hi type="italic">Ros-ha Sana</hi> 23 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) or ארנים (Para iii. 8), is explained by the Talmud as ערי, sing. ערא, i.e., according to Aruch and Rashi, <hi type="italic">laurier</hi>, the berries of which are called <hi type="italic">baies</hi>. We have rendered it “fig,” according to the lxx and Jerome, since it will not do to follow the seductive guidance of the similarity in sound to <hi type="italic">ornus</hi> (which is hardly equivalent to ὀρεινός).<note placement="foot">The ἀρία of Theophrastus is probably <hi type="italic">quercus ilex</hi>, which is still called ἀρία; the <hi type="italic">laurus nobilis</hi> is now called βαΐηά, from the branches which serve instead of palm-branches.</note> <div eID="gen13409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13410" type="x-p"/> The description is genealogical, and therefore moves retrogressively, from the felling to the planting. והיה in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">Isa 44:15</reference></hi> refers to the felled and planted tree, and primarily to the ash. מהם (of such as these) is neuter, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>; at the same time, the prophet had the עצים (the wood, both as produce and material) in his mind. The repeated אף lays emphasis upon the fact, that such different things are done with the very same wood. It is sued for warming, and fore the preparation of food, as well as for making a god. On the verbs of adoration, <hi type="italic">hishtachăvâh</hi> (root <hi type="italic">shach</hi>, to sink, to settle down) and <hi type="italic">sâgad</hi>, which is only applied to idolatrous worship, and from which <hi type="italic">mes'gid</hi>, a mosque, is derived, see Holemann’s <hi type="italic">Bibelstudien</hi>, i. 3. למו may no doubt be take as a plural (= להם, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.5">Isa 30:5</reference>), “such things (<hi type="italic">taila</hi>) does he worship,” as Stier supposes; but it is probably pathetic, and equivalent to לו, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Isa 53:8</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.11.7">Psa 11:7</reference>; Ewald, §247,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). According to the double application of the wood mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">Isa 44:15</reference>, a distinction is drawn in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.16">Isa 44:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.17">Isa 44:17</reference> between the one half of the wood and the other. The repeated <hi type="italic">chetsyō</hi> (the half of it) in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.16">Isa 44:16</reference> refers to the first half, which furnishes not only fuel for burning, but shavings and coals for roasting and baking as well. And as a fire made for cooking warms quite as much as one made expressly for the purpose, the prophet dwells upon this benefit which the wood of the idol does confer. On the tone upon the last syllable of <hi type="italic">chammōthı̄</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>; and on the use of the word ראה as a comprehensive term, embracing every kind of sensation and perception, see my <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 234. Diagoras of Melos, a pupil of Democritus, once threw a wooden standing figure of Hercules into the fire, and said jocularly, “Come now, Hercules, perform thy thirteenth labour, and help me to cook the turnips.”
entries.6896ee14da1189828d614c09521a28c12120dc6f: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.18-Isa.44.19">Isa 44:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen13410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13411" type="x-p"/> So irrational is idolatry; but yet, through self-hardening, they have fallen under the judgment of hardness of heart (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9-Isa.6.10">Isa 6:9-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Isa 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.10">Isa 29:10</reference>), and have been given up to a reprobate mind (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom 1:28</reference>). <hi type="italic">“They perceive not, and do not understand: for their eyes are smeared over, so that they do not see; their hearts, so that they do not understand. And men take it not to heart, no perception and no understanding, that men should say, The half of it I have burned in the fire, and also baked bread upon the coals thereof; roasted flesh, and eaten: and ought I to make the rest of it an abomination, to fall down before the produce of a tree?”</hi> Instead of טח, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.42">Lev 14:42</reference>, the third person is written טח (from <hi type="italic">tâchach</hi>, Ges. §72, Anm. 8) in a circumstantial sense: their eyes are, as it were, smeared over with plaster. The expression אל־לב השׁיב or על־לב (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.8">Isa 46:8</reference>), literally to carry back into the heart, which we find as well as על־לב שׂים, to take to heart (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>), answers exactly to the idea of reflection, here with reference to the immense contrast between a piece of wood and the Divine Being. The second and third לא in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">Isa 44:19</reference> introduce substantive clauses, just as verbal clauses are introduced by ואין. לאמר is used in the same manner as in <reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference> : “perception and insight showing themselves in their saying.” On <hi type="italic">būl</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Job.40.20">Job 40:20</reference>; the meaning “block” cannot be established: the talmudic <hi type="italic">būl</hi>, a lump or piece, which Ewald adduces, is the Greek βῶλος.
entries.614424a7f0769cd16e2231272df1b5150c3253b2: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.20">Isa 44:20</reference> <div eID="gen13411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13412" type="x-p"/> This exposure of the infatuation of idolatry closes with an epiphonem in the form of a gnome (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.26.7">Isa 26:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa 26:10</reference>). <hi type="italic">“He who striveth after ashes, a befooled heart has led him astray, and he does not deliver his soul, and does not think, Is there not a lie in my right hand?”</hi> We have here a complete and self-contained sentence, which must not be broken up in the manner proposed by Knobel, “He hunts after ashes; his heart is deceived,” etc. He who makes ashes, i.e., things easily scattered, perishable, and worthless, the object of his effort and striving (compare <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi> in Hos 12:2), has bee led astray from the path of truth and salvation by a heart overpowered by delusion; he is so certain, that he does not think of saving his soul, and it never occurs to him to say, “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” All that belongs to idolatry is <hi type="italic">sheqer</hi> - a fabrication and a lie. רעה means primarily to pasture or tend, hence to be concerned about, to strive after. הותל is an attributive, from <hi type="italic">tâlal</hi> - <hi type="italic">hâtal</hi>, <hi type="italic">ludere</hi>, <hi type="italic">ludificare</hi> (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa 30:10</reference>).
entries.e2b113db7414bdfcdb9681c75139c9326a27e04d: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.21-Isa.44.22">Isa 44:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen13412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13413" type="x-p"/> The second half of the prophecy commences with Isa 44:21. It opens with an admonition. <hi type="italic">“Remember this, Jacob and Israel; for thou art my servant: I have formed thee; thou art servant to me, O Israel: thou art not forgotten by me.”</hi> The thing to which the former were blind - namely, that idolatry is a lie - Jacob was to have firmly impressed upon its mind. The words “and Israel,” which are attached, are a contract for “and remember this, O Israel” (compare the vocatives after <hi type="italic">Vâv</hi> in <reference osisRef="Prov.8.5">Pro 8:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Joel.2.23">Joe 2:23</reference>). In the reason assigned, the tone rests upon <hi type="italic">my</hi> in the expression “my servant,” and for this reason “servant to me” is used interchangeably with it. Israel is the servant of Jehovah, and as such it was formed by Jehovah; and therefore reverence was due to Him, and Him alone. The words which follow are rendered by the lxx, Targum, Jerome, and Luther as though they read לא תנשׁני, though Hitzig regards the same rendering as admissible even with the reading תנּשנּי, inasmuch as the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> נשּׁה has the middle sense of ἐπιλανθάνεσθαι, <hi type="italic">oblivisci</hi>. But it cannot be shown that <hi type="italic">nizkar</hi> is ever used in the analogous sense of μιμνήσκεσθαι, <hi type="italic">recordari</hi>. The <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, which was no doubt originally reflective, is always used in Hebrew to indicate simply the passive endurance of something which originated with the subject of the action referred to, so that <hi type="italic">nisshâh</hi> could only signify “to forget one’s self.” We must indeed admit the possibility of the meaning “to forget one’s self” having passed into the meaning “to be forgetful,” and this into the meaning “to forget.” The Aramaean תנשׁי also signifies to be forgotten and (with an accent following) to forget, and the connection with an objective suffix has a support in ויּלּחמוּני in Psa 109:3. But the latter is really equivalent to אתּי וילחמו, so that it may be adduced with equal propriety in support of the other rendering, according to which תּנּשׁני is equivalent to לי תנש (Ges., Umbr., Ewald, Stier). There are many examples of this brachyological use of the suffix (Ges. §121, 4), so that this rendering is certainly the safer of the two. It also suits the context quite as well as the former, “Oh, forget me not;” the assurance “thou wilt not be forgotten by me” (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.49.15">Isa 49:15</reference> and the lamentation of Israel in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa 40:27</reference>) being immediately followed by an announcement of the act of love, by which the declaration is most gloriously confirmed. - <reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">Isa 44:22</reference> <hi type="italic">“I have blotted out thy transgressions as a mist, and thy sins as clouds: return to me; for I have redeemed thee.”</hi> We have adopted the rendering “mist” merely because we have no synonym to “cloud;” we have not translated it “thick cloud,” because the idea of darkness, thickness, or opacity, which is the one immediately suggested by the word, had become almost entirely lost (see <reference osisRef="Isa.25.5">Isa 25:5</reference>). Moreover, קל עב is evidently intended here (see <reference osisRef="Isa.19.1">Isa 19:1</reference>), inasmuch as the point of comparison is not the dark, heavy multitude of sins, but the facility and rapidity with which they are expunged. Whether we connect with מסהיתי the idea of a stain, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.51.3">Psa 51:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.11">Psa 51:11</reference>, or that of a debt entered in a ledge, as in <reference osisRef="Col.2.14">Col 2:14</reference>, and as we explained it in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference> (cf., <hi type="italic">mâchâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.32-Exod.32.33">Exo 32:32-33</reference>), in any case sin is regarded as something standing between God and man, and impeding or disturbing the intercourse between them. This Jehovah clears away, just as when His wind sweeps away the clouds, and restores the blue sky again (<reference osisRef="Job.26.13">Job 26:13</reference>). Thus does God’s free grace now interpose at the very time when Israel thinks He has forgotten it, blotting out Israel’s sin, and proving this by redeeming it from a state of punishment. What an evangelical sound the preaching of the Old Testament evangelist has in this passage also! Forgiveness and redemption are not offered on condition of conversion, but the mercy of God comes to Israel in direct contrast to what its works deserve, and Israel is merely called upon to reciprocate this by conversion and renewed obedience. The perfects denote that which has essentially taken place. Jehovah has blotted out Israel’s sin, inasmuch as He does not impute it any more, and thus has redeemed Israel. All that yet remains is the outward manifestation of this redemption, which is already accomplished in the counsel of God.
entries.9547537e82e9970df6132f450e185b73086f80d0: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Isa 44:23</reference> <div eID="gen13413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13414" type="x-p"/> There is already good ground, therefore, for exuberant rejoicing; and the reply of the church to these words of divine consolation is as follows: <hi type="italic">“Exult, O heavens; for Jehovah hath accomplished it: shout, ye depths of the earth; break out, ye mountains, into exulting; thou forest, and all the wood therein: for Jehovah hath redeemed Jacob, and He showeth Himself glorious upon Israel.”</hi> All creation is to rejoice in the fact that Jehovah has completed what He purposed, that He has redeemed His people, and henceforth will show Himself glorious in them. The heavens on high are to exult; also the depths of the earth, i.e., not Hades, which would be opposed to the prevailing view of the Old Testament (Ps 66, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.88.13">Psa 88:13</reference>), but the interior of the earth, with its caves, its pits, and its deep abysses (see <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15">Psa 139:15</reference>); and the mountains and woods which rise up from the earth towards heaven - all are to unite in the exultation of the redeemed: for the redemption that is being accomplished in man will extend its effects in all directions, even to the utmost limits of the natural world. <div eID="gen13414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13415" type="x-p"/> This exulting finale is a safe boundary-stone of this fifth prophecy. It opened with “Thus saith the Lord,” and the sixth opens with the same.
entries.df5835d53bdbc697a0794b644b436b16df3fc549: <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24-Isa.44.28">Isa 44:24-28</reference> <div eID="gen13415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13416" type="x-p"/> The promise takes a new turn here, acquiring greater and greater speciality. It is introduced as the word of Jehovah, who first gave existence to Israel, and has not let it go to ruin. <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah, thy Redeemer, and He that formed thee from the womb, I Jehovah am He that accomplisheth all; who stretched out the heavens alone, spread out the earth by Himself; who bringeth to nought the signs of the prophets of lies, and exposeth the soothsayers as raging mad; who turneth back the wise men, and maketh their science folly; who realizeth the word of His servant, and accomplisheth the prediction of His messengers; who saith to Jerusalem, She shall be inhabited! and to the cities of Judah, They shall be built, and their ruins I raise up again! who saith to the whirlpool, Dry up; and I dry its streams! who saith to Koresh, My shepherd and he will perform all my will; and will say to Jerusalem, She shall be built, and the temple founded!”</hi> The prophecy which commences with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference></hi> is carried on through this group of vv. in a series of participial predicates to אנכי (I) Jehovah is <hi type="italic">‛ōseh</hi> <hi type="italic">kōl</hi>, accomplishing all (<hi type="italic">perficiens omnia</hi>), so that there is nothing that is not traceable to His might and wisdom as the first cause. It was He who alone, without the co-operation of any other being, stretched out the heavens, who made the earth into a wide plain by Himself, i.e., so that it proceeded from Himself alone: מאתּי, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.11.20">Jos 11:20</reference> (compare מני, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">Isa 30:1</reference>; and <hi type="italic">mimmennı̄</hi> in Hos 8:4), <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> אתּי מי, “who was with me,” or “who is it beside me?” The Targum follows the <hi type="italic">keri</hi>; the Septuagint the <hi type="italic">chethib</hi>, attaching it to the following words, τίς ἕτερος διασκεδάσει. <reference osisRef="Isa.44.25">Isa 44:25</reference> passes on from Him whom creation proves to be God, to Him who is proving Himself to be so in history also, and that with obvious reference to the Chaldean soothsayers and wise men (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.9-Isa.47.10">Isa 47:9-10</reference>), who held out to proud Babylon the most splendid and hopeful prognostics. “<hi type="italic">Who brings to nought</hi> (<hi type="italic">mēphēr</hi>, opp. <hi type="italic">mēqı̄m</hi>) <hi type="italic">the signs</hi>,” i.e., the marvellous proofs of their divine mission which the false prophets adduced by means of fraud and witchcraft. The lxx render <hi type="italic">baddı̄m</hi>, ἐγγαστριμύθων, Targ. <hi type="italic">bı̄dı̄n</hi> (in other passages = <hi type="italic">'ōb</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.27">Lev 20:27</reference>; <hi type="italic">'ōbōth</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.31">Lev 19:31</reference>; hence = πύθων πύθωνες). At <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.11.3">Job 11:3</reference> we have derived it as a common noun from בּדה = בּטא, to speak at random; but it is possible that בּדה may originally have signified to produce or bring forth, without any reference to βαττολογεῖν, then to invent, to fabricate, so that <hi type="italic">baddı̄m</hi> as a personal name (as in <reference osisRef="Jer.50.36">Jer 50:36</reference>) would be synonymous with <hi type="italic">baddâ'ı̄m</hi>, <hi type="italic">mendaces</hi>. On <hi type="italic">qōsemı̄m</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Isa.3.2">Isa 3:2</reference>; on <hi type="italic">yehōlēl</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job 12:17</reference>, where it occurs in connection with a similar predicative description of God according to His works. <div eID="gen13416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13417" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa 44:26</reference> a contrast is draw between the heathen soothsayers and wise men, and the servant and messengers of Jehovah, whose word, whose <hi type="italic">‛ētsâh</hi>, i.e., determination or disclosure concerning the future (cf., <hi type="italic">yâ‛ats</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.28">Isa 41:28</reference>), he realizes and perfectly fulfils. By “his servant” we are to understand Israel itself, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.42.19">Isa 42:19</reference>, but only relatively, namely, as the bearer of the prophetic word, and therefore as the kernel of Israel regarded from the standpoint of the prophetic mission which it performed; and consequently “his messengers” are the prophets of Jehovah who were called out of Israel. The singular “his servant” is expanded in “his messenger” into the plurality embraced in the one idea. This is far more probable than that the author of these prophetic words, who only speaks of himself in a roundabout manner even in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Isa 40:6</reference>, should here refer directly to himself (according to <reference osisRef="Isa.20.3">Isa 20:3</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa 44:26</reference></hi> the predicates become special prophecies, and hence their outward limits are also defined. As we have תּוּשׁב and not תּוּשׁבי, we must adopt the rendering <hi type="italic">habitetur</hi> and <hi type="italic">oedificentur</hi>, with which the continuation of the latter <hi type="italic">et vastata ejus erigam</hi> agrees. In <reference osisRef="Isa.44.27">Isa 44:27</reference> the prophecy moves back from the restoration of Jerusalem and the cities of Judah to the conquest of Babylon. The expression calls to mind the drying up of the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.10">Isa 51:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.16">Isa 43:16</reference>); but here it relates to something future, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.42.15">Isa 42:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference> -namely, to the drying up of the Euphrates, which Cyrus turned into the enlarged basin of Sepharvaim, so that the water sank to the depth of a single foot, and men could “go through on foot” (Herod. i. 191). But in the complex view of the prophet, the possibility of the conqueror’s crossing involved the possibility or the exiles’ departing from the prison of the imperial city, which was surrounded by a natural and artificial line of waters (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Isa 11:15</reference>). צוּלה (from צוּל = צלל, to whiz or whirl) refers to the Euphrates, just as <hi type="italic">metsūlâh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.41.23">Job 41:23</reference>; Zec 10:11, does to the Nile; נתרריה is used in the same sense as the Homeric ̓Ωοκεάνοιο ῥέεθρα. In <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa 44:28</reference> the special character of the promise reaches its highest shoot. The deliverer of Israel is mentioned by name: “That saith to Koresh, My shepherd (i.e., a ποιμὴν λαῶν appointed by me), and he who performs all my will” (<hi type="italic">chēphets</hi>, θέλημα, not in the generalized sense of πρᾶγμα), and that inasmuch as he (Cyrus) saith to (or of) Jerusalem, It shall be built (<hi type="italic">tibbâneh</hi>, not the second pers. <hi type="italic">tibbânı̄</hi>), and the foundation of the temple laid (<hi type="italic">hēkhâl</hi> a masculine elsewhere, here a feminine). This is the passage which is said by Josephus to have induced Cyrus to send back the Jews to their native land: “Accordingly, when Cyrus read this, and admired the divine power, an earnest desire and ambition seized upon him to fulfil what was so written” (Jos. <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> xi. 2). According to Ctesias and others, the name of Cyrus signifies the sun.But all that can really be affirmed is, that it sounds like the name of the sun. For in Neo-Pers. the sun is called <hi type="italic">char</hi>, in Zendic <hi type="italic">hvarĕ</hi> (<hi type="italic">karĕ</hi>), and from this proper names are formed, such as <hi type="italic">chars'ı̂d</hi> (Sunshine, also the Sun); but Cyrus is called <hi type="italic">Kuru</hi> or <hi type="italic">Khuru</hi> upon the monuments, and this cannot possibly be connected with our <hi type="italic">chur</hi>, which would be <hi type="italic">uwara</hi> in Old Persian (Rawlinson, Lassen, Spiegel), and <hi type="italic">Kōresh</hi> is simply the name of <hi type="italic">Kuru</hi> (Κῦρ-ος) Hebraized after the manner of a segholate. There is a marble-block, for example, in the Murghab valley, not far from the mausoleum of Cyrus, which contained the golden coffin with the body of the king (see Strabo, xv 3, 7); and on this we find an inscription that we also meet with elsewhere, viz., <hi type="italic">adam</hi>. <hi type="italic">k'ur'us</hi>.<hi type="italic">khsâya</hi> | <hi type="italic">thiya</hi>.<hi type="italic">hakhâmanisiya</hi>, i.e., I am Kuru the king of the Achaemenides.<note placement="foot">See the engraving of this tomb of Cyrus, which is now called the “Tomb of Solomon’s mother,” in Vaux’s <hi type="italic">Nineveh and Persepolis</hi> (p. 345). On the identity of <hi type="italic">Murghâb</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pasargadae</hi>, see Spiegel, <hi type="italic">Keil-inschriften</hi>, pp. 71, 72; and with regard to the discovery of inscriptions that may still be expected around the tomb of Cyrus, the J<hi type="italic">ournal of the Asiatic Society</hi>, x. 46, note 4 (also compare Spiegel’s <hi type="italic">Geschichte der Entzifferung der Keil-schrift, im “Ausland,”</hi> 1865, p. 413).</note> <div eID="gen13417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13418" type="x-p"/> This name is identical with the name of the river <hi type="italic">Kur</hi> (Κῦρ-ος); and what Strabo says is worthy of notice - namely, that “there is also a river called Cyrus, which flows through the so-called cave of Persis near Pasargadae, and whence the king took his name, changing it from Agradates into Cyrus” (Strab. xv 3, 6). It is possible also that there may be some connection between the name and the Indian princely title of <hi type="italic">Kuru</hi>.  <chapter eID="Isa.44"/> <div eID="gen13418" type="x-p"/>

entries.857065c2ec5d2185c60ad0104f623ca6343226e8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.44.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.44.1" sID="gen48759" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet now hear. </hi>Having a little before rebuked the transgressions of the people, and declared that all deserved eternal perdition, because both the princes and the people had polluted everything by their crimes, he now mitigates that severity of punishment, and comforts the people. In this passage I consider the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign> <hi type="italic">(vau) </hi>to mean <hi type="italic">But </hi>or <hi type="italic">Yet, </hi>as in many other passages. As if he had said, “Though grievous afflictions are about to overtake thee, <hi type="italic">yet now </hi>hear what I will do for thy sake.” The verse must be viewed in connection with the former argument, because the Lord declares that he will never permit his people to perish altogether, though they be grievously afflicted. Hence infer, that God is never so angry with his Church as not to leave some room for mercy, as we have already seen on many occasions. The consequence is, that the prophets, whenever they threaten, always add some consolation as an abatement.<div eID="gen48760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48761" type="x-p"/>But lest we should imagine that men have deserved it by their good conduct, he therefore adds, <hi type="italic">whom I have chosen; </hi>for we do not serve God, because we are entitled to it, or deserve it, but because he renders us fit by a free election. In this passage, therefore, the words <hi type="italic">Servant </hi>and <hi type="italic">Elect </hi>are synonymous, yet so that election comes first in order, and therefore David says that he was God’s “servant” before he was born, because even from his mother’s womb he had been received into God’s family. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.10 Bible:Ps.71.6 Bible:Ps.116.16">Psalm 22:10; 71:6; 116:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen48761" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.44.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48759" osisID="Isa.44.1" type="section"/>
entries.c3460cb6fc50db1ad4904c9a55c41b7d5a773ec4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.44.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.44.2" sID="gen48762" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi><hi type="italic"> Thus saith Jehovah thy Maker. </hi>Though he treated the Jews harshly, that they might be stripped of all false confidence, and might humbly betake themselves to the grace of God, he now caresses them pleasantly by a mild and gentle discourse, that they may know that by self-denial they shall sustain no loss. We must therefore supply here the following contrasts. “Thou, Jacob, art indeed nothing in thyself, but God thy Maker will not despise his work; no nobleness of birth would secure thee against perdition, but the adoption which the Heavenly Father has been pleased to bestow upon thee will be abundantly sufficient for redeeming thee.” Besides, we should keep in mind what I have often said already, that the Prophet does not speak of the first creation by which we are born to be human beings, but of the regeneration which belongs and is peculiar to the elect, that they may obtain a place in the Church of God.<div eID="gen48763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48764" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He that formed thee from the womb. </hi>This is added, that men may not claim anything for themselves, as if they had moved him to shew kindness to them. By these words he also exhibits to them a hereditary covenant, by which God separated them to be his inheritance “before they were born.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.11">Romans 9:11</reference>.) Some think that this refers to the person of Jacob, because, by taking hold of his brother’s foot, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.26">Genesis 25:26</reference>,) he gave a remarkable proof of his election; but this is a forced interpretation, and therefore I give a wider signification to these words, namely, that the Lord was kind and bountiful to his people from the commencement, and cut off all merits; because by free grace he “formed him,” and then freely bestowed on him all blessings.<div eID="gen48764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48765" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He will help thee. </hi>Some supply the relative, <hi type="italic">“Who </hi>will help thee;” as if he had said, “Thy Helper;” but it is better to read the clause separately. <note n="173"> <div sID="gen48766" type="x-p"/> “Even on the common supposition, that the words of God begin with the second clause, it is better to take ‘He will help thee’ as a short independent clause, parenthetically thrown in to complete the description, or to connect it with what follows.” —<hi type="italic"> Alexander.</hi><div eID="gen48766" type="x-p"/> </note> It would be still more clear in the first person, “I will help thee;” but as to the substance of the meaning it makes no difference. The statemen t amounts to this, that he who is the Creator of the people will be ready to give his assistance when the proper time shall arrive. Let every person therefore adopt that reading which he thinks proper; but I have preferred to follow the simple and natural meaning, without supplying any word.<div eID="gen48765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48767" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">O beloved! </hi>The word <foreign xml:lang="he">ישרון</foreign> <hi type="italic">(yeshurun) </hi>is explained in various ways. Some think that it is derived from <foreign xml:lang="he">ישר</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(yashar,) </hi>which means “to be upright,” or “to please;” others from <foreign xml:lang="he">שור</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(shur,) </hi>and others from <foreign xml:lang="he">אשר</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(ashar.) </hi>But I rather agree with those who translate it <hi type="italic">Beloved, </hi>and derive it from the root <foreign xml:lang="he">ישר</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(yashar.) </hi>This designation is also bestowed on that nation by Moses in his song; for, although some render it in that passage <hi type="italic">Upright, </hi>and in this passage also, the old rendering is more suitable, “My beloved is grown fat.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.15">Deuteronomy 32:15</reference>.) The Prophet adorns his nation with these titles, that the Jews may be led by past benefits to entertain hope for the future. This rule ought to be held by all believers as perpetually binding, that, after having experienced the kindness of God toward them, they should likewise expect it for the future; for otherwise they will be excessively ungrateful, and will shew that they do not rely on the promises of God, which, when they are impressed on our hearts, undoubtedly bring peace and safety; not that we should be utterly devoid of fear, but that we should strive against all dread and distrust; and therefore he again repeats, —<div eID="gen48767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48768" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Fear thou not, Jacob. </hi>Such is also the import of the consolation given by Christ,<div eID="gen48768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48769" type="x-p"/>“Fear not, little flock, for my Father hath good will towards thee.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.32">Luke 12:32</reference>.)<div eID="gen48769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48770" type="x-p"/>And, indeed, among the dangers which threaten death on all sides, no remedy is better adapted to allay terrors than that God has been pleased to bestow his favor upon us, so that he will save us for ever. By the word “Beloved,” therefore, he again repeats that this depends on the favor and protection of God, who ascribes to himself, and entirely claims, all the good that existed among the people.<div eID="gen48770" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.44.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48762" osisID="Isa.44.2" type="section"/>
entries.63785cee6beefed1c05e79c69ce94c7b5fcd8eac: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.44.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.44.3" sID="gen48771" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi><hi type="italic"> For I will pour waters. </hi>He continues the same subject, and at the same time explains what will be the nature of that assistance which he has promised. But we ought always to keep in remembrance that these prophecies relate to that sorrowful and afflicted period of which he formerly spoke, that is, when the people, in the extremity to which they were reduced, might think that they were altogether forsaken, and that all the promises of God were vain. Isaiah meets this doubt, and compares the people to a dry and thirsty land, which has no moisture at all. By this metaphor David also describes his wretchedness. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.143.6">Psalm 143:6</reference>.) Although therefore they were worn out by afflictions, and the vital moisture was decayed, yet, that they might not throw away courage in their deepest distresses, they ought to have set before their minds this declaration of the Prophet.
